Poland has detained and charged three teenagers who are allegedly linked to “an international neo-Nazi network” and had been planning terrorist attacks, including with the use of homemade explosives.

The arrests were announced on Monday morning by Tomasz Siemoniak, the minister in charge of the security services, who revealed that the suspects are Polish citizens. Two are aged 17 and one is 16.

“The teenagers not only promoted Nazi and fascist ideology but had also already taken steps toward committing terrorist offences,” wrote Siemoniak.

Funkcjonariusze @ABW_GOV_PL zatrzymali 3 obywateli RP, 16-latka i dwóch 17-latków, związanych z międzynarodowym środowiskiem neonazistowskim.
▶️ Nastolatkowie nie tylko propagowali ideologię nazistowską i faszystowską, ale podejmowali już działania zmierzające do popełniania…

— Tomasz Siemoniak (@TomaszSiemoniak) November 16, 2026

The National Prosecutor’s Office revealed that the trio were “fascinated by the activities of an international neo-Nazi terrorist organisation…[that] has an ideology based on hatred against people of Jewish descent, immigrants, black people, the LGBT community, politicians and state security officials”.

Though prosecutors did not name the organisation, they said that members of it have been involved in planning terrorist attacks in the United States, Germany and the United Kingdom. In some countries, including the UK, Canada and Australia, it has been outlawed and designated a terrorist group.

Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW) had found that the three suspects’ online communication indicated “an interest in constructing explosive devices, modifying weapons and using such items to carry out terrorist activities”.

During a search of the home of one of the 17-year-olds (named only as “suspect 1”), officers found chemicals that are precursors for the production of explosives. That suspect has also been charged with possession of a so-called pipe bomb, which prosecutors say he wanted to “transfer to a neo-Nazi terrorist group”.

 

Suspect 1 was found to have discussed with the other 17-year-old, named as suspect 2, how to construct an explosive device and detonate it in a specific residential building where someone they knew lived.

Suspect 1 had also “incited extremist behaviour and hate-motivated violence” in his online activity, while the 16-year-old, named as suspect 3, had “promoted fascist content” (a crime in Poland) and encouraged someone to assault another person based on their race.

Each suspect has been charged with three crimes, relating variously to terrorist offences, possession or attempted production of explosives and weapons, promoting Nazism, fascism and racial hatred, and inciting others to commit violence based on racial differences.

Prosecutors note that Polish law generally allows people to face full criminal liability from the age of 17. The two 17-year-olds have therefore been placed in adult pretrial detention, while the 16-year-old is being held in a juvenile facility.

Śledztwo w sprawie neonazistów i planowanych aktów terroru kryminalnego

Szczegóły w komunikacie: ⬇️https://t.co/dQpdgiTYJD

— Prokuratura Regionalna w Gdańsku (@Prok_Regio_GDA) November 16, 2026

The arrests come in the context of recent concerns over radicalisation of young people in Poland. Earlier this month, a 24-year-old carried out a terrorist attack in the city of Kraków, killing six people by firing a rifle from his car. He had earlier killed his parents and sister in their home.

In the aftermath of the attack, justice minister Waldemar Żurek revealed that investigators had found “very strong traces of right-wing extremism” in the attacker’s online activity, though he emphasised that the motive was yet to be determined.

In the space of a few days last month, three knife attacks took place in Polish schools, resulting in one case in the death of a member of staff. Dozens of young people were arrested in the aftermath for making threats and/or possessing weapons.

In September, the security services detained three teenagers accused of being part of online groups promoting neo-Nazism and violence. One of them has been charged with planning terrorist attacks on targets including a mosque and a school.

]]> Ukraine blames Russia for graffiti glorifying WWII Ukrainian nationalists on Polish monuments https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/11/15/ukraine-blames-russia-for-graffiti-glorifying-wwii-ukrainian-nationalists-on-polish-monuments/ Sun, 15 Nov 2026 15:48:17 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=106807 Why are you now seeing adverts on our website for the first time? Around a dozen public monuments in Poland, including one dedicated to the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, have been defaced with graffiti glorifying the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), a World War Two nationalist partisan group that was responsible for the massacre of Poles and Jews.

Ukraine’s embassy in Warsaw has condemned the vandalism and blamed it on Russia, which has previously been accused by the Polish authorities of orchestrating provocative graffiti on monuments.

W sobotę, 14 listopada, w Warszawie doszło do kolejnych dwóch dewastacji pomników. Napisy „Slava UPA” pojawiły się na Pomniku Bohaterów Getta przed Muzeum Historii Żydów Polskich POLIN oraz na Pomniku Żołnierzy 1 Armii Wojska Polskiego przy ulicy Andersa 13. To kolejna odsłona… pic.twitter.com/Y7NDsfpjxn

— Miejski Reporter (@MiejskiReporter) November 14, 2026

The latest spate of vandalism was first reported in early November in the western city of Poznań, where three World War two memorials were painted with graffiti saying “Glory to the UPA” (Slawa UPA).

While the UPA is remembered by many in Ukraine for fighting for independence from Moscow-imposed Soviet rule, in Poland it is primarily associated with leading the Volhynia massacres, in which around 100,000 Polish civilians, mostly women and children, were slaughtered as part of an ethnic cleansing operation.

Local police in Poznań told the Gazeta Wyborcza daily that they were searching for a young man dressed in black who is believed to be the culprit, but have so far not been able to identify him.

 

Similar graffiti was subsequently reported on seven monuments, including ones dedicated to Polish World War Two heroes and anti-communist protests that took place in 1970, in Gdańsk and Gdynia, neighbouring cities on Poland’s northern Baltic coast.

On Friday, local police in Gdańsk confirmed that they had detained a 17-year-old Ukrainian on suspicion of “painting offensive slogans propagating hatred”. They shared blurred-out images of the suspect as well as cans of spray paint.

He has been charged with promoting fascist ideology, incitement to violence and hatred based on nationality, and desecration of monuments. If convicted, he could face up to three years in prison.

Previously, on Tuesday this week, MOST, a Polish-based Belarusian independent media outlet, published findings that an anonymous person on messaging service Telegram, which is popular among Russians, Ukrainians and Belarusians, had been offering $500 plus travel expenses for a job in Poznań.

When an undercover MOST journalist responded to the advert, he was told that the job would involve spray painting “Glory to the UPA” on monuments. The recruiter confirmed that the job was illegal, “but if you cover your face and do everything quickly, they won’t find you”.

They also revealed that similar jobs were available in other Polish cities, including Warsaw, Wrocław and Lublin.

Subsequently, similar inscriptions appeared in Warsaw on the Monument to the Ghetto Heroes, which honours the Jews who rose up against their German-Nazi oppressors in 1943; a monument commemorating the Polish First Army, which fought in World War Two; and a monument to sappers who served in the war.

The vandalism was condemned by Poland’s Jewish Historical Institute (ŻIH), which called it a “disgraceful attack on the memory of the victims of the Holocaust and the heroes of Jewish resistance”.

Noting MOST’s findings and the vandalism of other monuments, ŻIH said that “this points to the possibility of an organised provocation intended to incite hatred and divide society”.

Warsaw police told PAP that they are investigating and seeking to identify the perpetrator. An unnamed police source also told Gazeta Wyborcza they see the incidents in all four cities as related to one another, pointing to the similar style of the inscriptions.

On Sunday afternoon, Warsaw’s mayor, Rafał Trzaskowski, condemned the vandalism and shared images of the municipal authorities cleaning the graffiti off the Ghetto Heroes Monument.

“Given the scale of similar incidents in other cities, we must consider the possibility that this is a planned provocation,” added the mayor. “Let us not let ourselves be divided – the authorities are working to identify both those who carried out these acts and those who ordered them.”

Nie ma zgody na wandalizm w Warszawie.

Minionej nocy służby miejskie wyczyściły pomniki oszpecone przez wandali – między innymi Pomnik Bohaterów Getta. Sprawców szuka policja.

Patrząc na skalę podobnych incydentów w innych miastach, musimy brać pod uwagę, że mamy do czynienia… pic.twitter.com/5xMgPhnHf8

A day earlier, on Saturday, the Ukrainian embassy had also condemned the acts of vandalism, calling them a “disgraceful provocation”.

By Leo Greenberg

Speaking to Fox News in late October, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky admitted a widely known but uncomfortable truth: Ukraine needs its refugees back.

“We need 9.5 million people – who lost their homes, who are abroad, everywhere – we need them to come back to Ukraine…to rebuild their country,” he said.

Zelensky:

We need 9.5 million people who lost their housing, who are abroad everywhere — we need them to come back to Ukraine, just to live and to build their country. pic.twitter.com/Xu2Ld4eGOu

— Clash Report (@clashreport) October 21, 2026

Unfortunately for Ukraine, all signs point in the opposite direction: Ukrainians abroad are deferring or abandoning thoughts of return.

A large proportion of those refugees – almost one million of them – live in Poland, where Ukrainians, including migrants who arrived before 2022, have provided an economic and demographic boon. But their continued stay has also posed social and political challenges, as a country with no history of mass immigration grapples with the new reality of a sizable non-citizen minority.

This has left the refugees themselves in a state of limbo: torn between a homeland that wants them back, and to which many would like to return, but where conditions do not allow for it; and an adopted home where they have created new lives but where social tensions and logistical hurdles have meant persistent uncertainty.

A new reality sets in

When Solomiia Pischana, a Ukrainian woman in her late twenties, fled from Kyiv to Poland in the wake of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, she hoped to go back that same year.

When Kyiv was secured by Ukrainian forces, a return seemed possible. In late 2022, Pischana started travelling back home to see family and friends. “I was really living between two countries. I thought a lot about going back.”

Yet quickly, a new reality set in on her visits: “In winter it became basically impossible to stay there – the constant explosions.” In Poland, by contrast, “everyone put the emphasis on helping me, on helping Ukrainians.”

In a photo essay, we look at the lives of three of the million or so Ukrainian refugees who remain in Poland one year on from Russia's invasion: Liudmyla, a mother; Vlad, an amputee soldier; and Viktoria, a high-school student https://t.co/kdOpEgt2LB

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 21, 2023

For many Ukrainians, Pischana’s story will feel familiar. When Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Poland became the main waystation for Ukrainians on their way out. Millions crossed the border, and while many went on to other destinations in Europe and beyond, initially more than one million remained in Poland.

The Polish state reacted quickly, assigning more than a million special identification numbers for Ukrainian refugees – known as “PESEL-UKR” – and enrolling them in the same housing and benefits systems used by Polish citizens.

So too did Polish society, with a majority of Poles working in some way to assist Ukraine or arriving refugees, and many hosting refugees in their homes.

Around 77% of Poles have been involved in helping refugees from Ukraine, for which purpose they spent around €2 billion out of their own pockets, a new study by @PIE_NET_PL has found https://t.co/xWu8JWNMui

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 28, 2022

For Ukraine, the exodus of around six million refugees meant a raft of problems. Some 650,000 military-age men left the country, while schools had to figure out how to provide remote instruction for two million children abroad.

Most of all, the refugee crisis worsened Ukraine’s demographic challenges. Before 2022, Ukraine’s population of 42 million had already been shrinking and ageing. Now, Ukraine’s minister for social policy estimates that just 22-25 million people remain in Ukrainian-controlled territory. Two thirds of Ukrainian businesses are short of workers.

Initially, many hoped for a brief war. But, as the reality of a long, grinding conflict dawned, it became clear that Ukraine could no longer plan for an imminent influx of able-bodied adults: surveys by Kyiv’s Centre for Economic Strategies show that the proportion of refugees intending to return dropped from 74% in November 2022 to 43% in January 2026.

“Rather chaotic” attempts to connect with refugees

This reality has meant that, while Ukraine needs its people back, it also knows that it cannot compel people to return to a life defined by rolling blackouts and the ever-present threat of drones and ballistic missiles.

As a result, Ukraine’s efforts to encourage and support refugee return have been haphazard and limited.

Ukraine has one deputy minister, Ilona Havronska, who is armed with just 150 million hryvnia (13.1 million zloty, €3 million) in this year’s state budget to maintain connections with refugees abroad and support their return.

Havronska has sought to create a network of “Unity Hubs,” paid for by foreign governments, where Ukrainian refugees can confer with trained consultants about returning home. Such facilities have opened in Stockholm, Prague and Berlin, with the latter receiving 5,000 visits since opening in May.

⚡️Ukraine, Germany agree to open 'Unity Hub' for Ukrainian refugees in Berlin.

"This is a professional space that brings together community, business, and cultural initiatives," National Unity Minister Oleksii Chernyshov said.https://t.co/rlTq3MpOd0

— The Kyiv Independent (@KyivIndependent) February 15, 2025

So far, however, no hub has opened in Poland, whose interior ministry told Notes from Poland: “To be frank, the Ukrainian side, Minister Havronska, they haven’t approached us much about this recently.”

Ukraine’s other major effort, a digital platform called “Dodomu” (“Homeward”), allows users to make a return plan and check off items on a digital to-do list, such as transferring medical files, verifying IDs, and registering children in Ukrainian schools.

Since launching in June, Dodomu has been used by 4,500 people in Poland, of whom 600 have completed a questionnaire about their possibility of return.

Ukraine’s efforts to reach out to refugees abroad have been “rather chaotic”, according to Olena Babakova, a Polish-Ukrainian journalist and researcher who studies migration.

 

However, a survey by the UNHCR suggests that it may not make much difference: Ukrainian refugees ranked “support for return” as less important to their decision-making than security, economic opportunities, and housing in Ukraine. Nevertheless, for older refugees and those from now-occupied territories in eastern Ukraine, large numbers cited additional information as one of their key needs.

Valentina Bryl, a Ukrainian who has lived in Poland since before 2022 and is now an HR specialist in Wrocław, notes that returning to Ukraine would mean she would have to “start everything from the beginning – my job, my life. It’s not just about safety.”

So while Bryl says that she visits Ukraine often – taking the 25-hour rail journey from Wrocław to Kharkiv to see her husband, who is serving at the front – she hasn’t made use of Dodomu or thought about the Unity Hubs. She has no intention of moving back.

From welcome to wariness in Poland

Yet for the million or so Ukrainian refugees in Poland, as well as the hundreds of thousands of Ukrainian economic migrants who came before 2022, a growing consideration is not only the conditions in Ukraine, but also the environment they face in their adopted homeland.

Poland welcomed refugees in 2022 and has supported them since. It has also benefited economically from their presence, with Ukrainian refugees estimated to have raised national GDP by 2.4% in 2025.

Ukrainian refugees boosted Poland’s GDP by 2.4% in 2025, the equivalent of €21.5bn, according to a report by the UN @Refugees agency and @Deloitte

At the same time, their growing presence in the labour market had no negative impact on employment or wages https://t.co/lcsuIwBzpy

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 8, 2026

However, there have been growing social and political tensions. During the 2025 presidential election, even liberal candidates proposed restricting child benefits for Ukrainian refugees.

The eventual winner, right-wing candidate Karol Nawrocki, in one of his first acts as president, vetoed an extension of Ukrainians’ temporary protections, before signing a revised extension that restricted benefits.

Those political changes reflect shifting attitudes in society. A June 2026 report from the Institute of Political Critique (IKP) described last year’s election campaign as a “Rubicon”, citing testimony from Ukrainian refugees that the public environment had become more hostile and historical issues had surfaced.

Pischana told Notes from Poland that, while she is “surrounded by good people” in Poland, she has noticed that “old topics like the Volhynia massacre are coming up much more”, referring to the mass slaughter of Poles by Ukrainian nationalists in World War Two. “Just walking down the street and speaking Ukrainian, it’s started to feel a bit more dangerous,” she added.

Police data show that the number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland was 30% higher in the first half of this year than in the same period of 2025.

The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland is up 30% so far this year, police data show.

The figures come following recent high-profile cases of verbal and physical attacks against Ukrainians, who are Poland's largest immigrant group https://t.co/pcTsJddDz7

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 17, 2026

Myroslava Keryk, who leads Ukraiński Dom, a hub that provides services to Ukrainian refugees in Warsaw, told Notes from Poland that her staff have faced growing harassment.

She described a slew of AI-generated videos depicting them demanding Poles pay greater taxes to support refugees, as well as sexualised, fake accounts made of her employees on online apps.

Poland’s government has condemned the recent spate of hate crimes and accused the opposition and Nawrocki of stirring up such social vitriol. Meanwhile, it has begun preparing for Ukrainian refugees’ longer-term stay.

Ukrainian refugees’ current PESEL-UKR status is tied to the EU’s temporary protections, now set to expire in March 2028. So this year, the government introduced a new “CUKR” status, valid for three years of residence after it is granted. Some 75,000 Ukrainians have already submitted applications.

President Nawrocki has signed into law a government bill ending the special status granted in 2022 to Ukrainian refugees, who will now be treated on the same legal basis as other foreigners.

Nawrocki said he is "ending the era of unconditional privileges" https://t.co/BzY7wrdl49

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 20, 2026

This new status, however, is only a step on the path to long-term stability. CUKR, unlike most refugees’ current “UKR” status, counts toward the five years of legal stay required to apply for long-term EU resident status. However, its three-year duration means holders need to secure two additional years of legal protection in Poland before applying for long-term residency.

Polish state policies have not always made things easy for refugees. New restrictions on benefits and on travel outside of Poland have made refugees careful. Despite that, many appreciated the legal and logistical clarity of Poland’s approach, typified by the new CUKR status.

Refugees’ primary fears have concerned their social environment, not their legal status. Babakova put it neatly: “Ukrainians in Poland feel very connected to Ukrainian society, but not the state. At the same time, they have come to trust the Polish state, but not Polish society.”

The citizenship question

At the same time, a growing number of Ukrainians are thinking of obtaining citizenship, which would allow them to travel more freely and vote in Polish elections.

An August survey of Ukrainian refugees in Poland found that a plurality (35%) listed obtaining citizenship as the “most desired form of assistance” to make their lives easier.

In 2025, a record 19,000 foreigners, more than half of whom (10,000) were Ukrainian, were granted citizenship in Poland.

Poland granted citizenship to a record 19,135 foreigners in 2025, up 17% from the previous year and almost five times higher than a decade ago.

Over half of recipients were Ukrainians, followed by Belarusians, Russians, Vietnamese and Turks https://t.co/FoyWd5UPJx

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 15, 2026

But since then, Poland has moved to restrict access to citizenship – to make it “an earned privilege, not a formal certificate”, in the words of the interior ministry.

The plans include extending the required period of legal residence from five to eight years, requiring a loyalty declaration, mandating advanced knowledge of Polish, and introducing an exam on Polish history and values.

Pischana wants to become a Polish citizen: “I’ve thought that it would be logical […] I’ve lived for years in Poland. I know the language.” She added that her university thesis focuses on Polish history: she’s writing a comparison of Ukrainian and Polish songs with political or social themes, from the 1980s to the present day.

Kamil Kisiel, deputy director for the department of internal affairs and migration at Poland’s interior ministry, told Notes from Poland that the new citizenship laws, soon to be announced, will be tough: “For now, being more restrictive is the way to go, so that we can manage people’s expectations”.

The proportion of Poles who hold a negative view of relations with Ukraine has risen to the highest level ever recorded by state research agency CBOS

Meanwhile, the proportion who believe reconciliation with Ukraine is possible is at its lowest ever level https://t.co/YYBCFkVxNr

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 12, 2026

Kisiel was also up front that the Polish government does not envision many Ukrainians in Poland becoming citizens. No more than a few tens of thousands of Ukrainians have obtained Polish citizenship in the past decade, and those who arrived in 2022 are not yet eligible to apply.

Instead, Kisiel highlighted, “long-term EU residence is…the sort of stability people should expect”.

Karina, a Ukrainian woman who has been in Poland since she was 15 and did not want her surname published, says that she wants Polish citizenship as it offers “a chance to travel around the European Union, go to Spain. You can also go to America, because a Polish passport gives you visa-free travel; unfortunately, with a Ukrainian one you can’t.”

Head in Poland, heart in Ukraine

Barring a major change in the course of the war, Ukraine may even become one of the countries, including Ireland and Armenia, whose diasporas are as large or larger than their domestic population – a scenario that Havronska, the Ukrainian deputy minister, told Notes from Poland she is planning for.

At the same time, social tensions and citizenship restrictions in Poland reflect the fact that refugees are challenging Poland’s identity: since the eradication and movement of Jews, Ukrainians and Germans during and after World War Two, Poland has been a largely monoethnic nation, accustomed to one language, one faith, and one national identity. The approximately 1.5 million Ukrainians in Poland have changed that.

For Pischana, her head is in Poland while her heart remains in Ukraine, saying that she feels more attached to the culture of her homeland. “It’s a pity I can’t develop in my own country, because there’s room to do it there,” she says.

For Bryl, it’s been harder to keep close to Ukraine: “I have work, I have other responsibilities…You no longer want to read, you don’t want to get angry at some bad news”.

At the beginning, she said, she felt she had a fully Ukrainian life – just one that was put on pause. But, she adds, “when it’s already been going on for five years, and it’s still unknown how long it’ll go on, well, it’s hard to keep it on pause.”

After Russia announced that it had dismantled a Polish spy network and arrested two alleged agents, Poland has dismissed the claims as “disinformation” and a “provocation”.

On Wednesday, while Poland was celebrating its national Independence Day, Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) announced that it had “disrupted the activities of an intelligence network of the Polish special services operating in Kaliningrad”, a Russian exclave that borders Poland.

It claimed to have detained two “agents”- one working for Poland’s Military Intelligence Service (SWW), the other for the Internal Security Agency (ABW) – who had been “collecting and transmitting information about military personnel and facilities” and “the socio-economic situation in the Kaliningrad region”.

 

The FSB added that seven Polish citizens and three Russians who had had contact with Polish intelligence agencies had been “officially warned”, and that the Polish citizens had been banned from entering Russia.

The agency also published a film containing images of alleged suspects being detained and various documents and telephone messages in Polish.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the arrests would not further worsen relations with Poland given ties between the two countries “essentially do not exist right now,” reported the RIA news agency.

 

In a statement on Wednesday morning, Jacek Dobrzyński, the spokesman for Poland’s security services, said that he regarded the Russian announcement “as yet another provocation and act of disinformation”, especially as it had been released on Polish Independence Day.

He added that he would not comment further and “appealed to everyone not to amplify hostile narratives or play into Russian propaganda”.

Speaking to news website Wirtualna Polska, Maciej Wewiór, the spokesman for Poland’s foreign ministry, said that Poland was working to verify the information announced by the FSB.

However, he urged “extreme caution” when dealing with such claims from Russia. “Let’s not fall for Russian propaganda and become pawns in this game,” he said.

The case dates back to before Bartoszewski had entered politics. In 2019, he became an MP for the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL). In 2023, after PSL became a junior partner in the current ruling coalition of Prime Minister Donald Tusk, he was made deputy foreign minister.

From 2004, say prosecutors, Bartoszewski was entrusted with managing the assets of Polish art collector and philanthropist Andrzej Ciechanowiecki, who was Bartoszewski’s godfather and a friend of his late father, Władysław Bartoszewski, a former Polish resistance fighter, Auschwitz prisoner, and later foreign minister.

The British Business Bank said it has had to “throw the kitchen sink at the problem” of financing Britain’s life sciences sector in a bid to draw in further investment from pension funds and help domestic firms scale in the UK.

The state lender’s financial backing for the sector has reached £1.1bn, including £832m spread across 20 life science funds, alongside £302m ploughed into numerous domestic scale-ups, to try and increase the size of funding rounds.

Recent investments included £25m in Alchemab Therapeutics, its biggest financial support provided to a life science firm to date, and £15m to Cambridge university spinout T-Therapeutics.

Hiking pension investment

Speaking to City AM, the bank’s chief investment officer, Leandros Kalisperas said the state lender had to “throw the kitchen sink at the problem” of financing life sciences as it works to encourage more investment from pension funds.

The bank has been attempting to entice institutional investors, including signatories of the Mansion House accord, to unlock further pension capital for private assets and venture capital firms, including those that invest in the life sciences sector.

The accord saw 11 of the UK’s top pension money managers commit to investing five per cent of their assets in private markets and unlisted equities by 2030.

“Backing life science innovation adds extra complexity. We are aiming…to communicate the possibilities for pension funds themselves to get involved,” Kalisperas said.

A recent update revealed that the vast majority of committed capital for UK private markets has been allocated to property, amounting to 70 per cent of the total £11.1bn.

In contrast, just £500m was invested into private equity.

Overseas assistance and AI cycle

The sector has also long been plagued by acquisitions and relocations driven by overseas buyers, who promise better funding and scaling conditions.

Companies from the bank’s portfolio have also not been immune to this trend. US pharmaceutical giant Merck & Co acquired ophthalmology biotech firm Eyebio in a deal worth up to $3bn (£2.2bn)  in 2024, while Japanese medical technology company Terumo snapped up Oxford University spinout Orgonox for $1.5bn last year.

But Chris Molloy, chief executive of the Bio Industry Association, said the increase in funding from the bank would “enable our most promising businesses to scale and stay in the UK”.

The lender also confirmed it committed €58m (£48.3m) to Sofinnova Crossover Fund II, a Parisian based fund which backs firms across Europe.

While the British Business Bank’s focus is on supporting domestic growth, Kalisperas said the state cannot rely solely on UK-only funds to attract deep pools of capital for specialist firms.

“You can’t back venture in the UK by just investing in managers that only invest in the UK,” he said.

“Within life sciences we have to acknowledge that there are European specialists in this space. We have to encourage them to invest in UK companies. Why wouldn’t we as a limited partner want them to do that?”

Looking ahead, Kalisperas expects investors to shift more capital into the sector as the AI cycle matures and products begin to implemented by real-world industries disconnected from the sector.

“People are going to be taking another look at life sciences because it is also linked in with AI… drug discovery can change through AI,” he added.

“I think there are a number of angles through which life sciences are hopefully going to get their moment.”

Canary Wharf development

The bank’s funding commitment follows the National Wealth Fund investing in one of London’s flagship science developments earlier this week.

It committed £147m of debt financing towards One North Quay in Canary Wharf, which will act as one of the “largest commercial science” buildings in Europe and address the lack of availability of specialist facilities needed to undertake research.

The financing is expected to fund the development of the project which is set to be completed in 2028. Barclays and Emirates NBD also pledged capital to the development, bringing the total to £368.5m.

Charles Avens, head of immigration at Collyer Bristow, said the absence of an investment-linked residency route was likely to divert capital towards competing jurisdictions, including Italy, the UAE and the US.

The MAC also recommended abolishing or fundamentally redesigning the Innovator Founder visa, introduced in 2023 to attract overseas entrepreneurs with scalable business ideas. Just over 700 people have entered Britain through the route since its launch.

“The median Innovator Founder business has roughly the turnover of a small independent coffee shop by the time visa holders apply for settlement,” the committee said.

Alan Milburn should be commended for his ambition to get NEETs back to work, but in the face of opposition from Labour backbenchers we could end up with more government intervention and subsidy while failing to address the perverse incentives in the welfare system, says Daniel Herring

Today, around 1m, or 13 per cent, of all 16-24 year olds are NEET (not in education, employment or training). Alan Milburn wants to dramatically reduce this to five per cent over a decade. This is a big task – while in countries like the Netherlands and Norway, it’s closer to five per cent, Britain’s figure has consistently stayed above 10 per cent for at least the last 25 years. 

So it is fair to say, as Milburn does, that the UK has a structural NEET problem, not just a cyclical one. Milburn’s report is detailed and comprehensive, but the report is an interesting mix of getting government out of the way, some tough love for young people, and then putting government back in the way again. 

On getting government out of the way, Milburn takes the government to task on employment costs. Milburn is right to point out that increasing the cost of hiring young people has harmed their employment prospects. Clearly, sharp rises in the minimum wage and employer national insurance are unhelpful for businesses. As the Centre for Policy Studies has shown recently, the rise in employment costs since Labour came to office is double that of inflation. 

Milburn rightly suggests reducing employer National Insurance, lightening the burden of regulation and slowing the rise of the minimum wage. These are welcome as a starting point.

Secondly, tough love in the welfare system. The report notes that the massive rise in health and disability benefits among young people “far outweighs the actual change in ill-health and disability”. Many people are acting rationally: they get more money from the welfare system than through employment. Clearly something is broken, with both the impact on young people’s lives and the fiscal cost becoming a millstone around the country’s neck. 

Most people would agree that “work beats welfare” for almost everyone. Milburn’s solution, to create a new youth allowance for anyone under 25 claiming either PIP or the health element of UC, is radical and welcome. Young people will also have a duty to engage or face losing the rest of their benefits. This reform is necessary, and again similar to that previously recommended by the CPS, but it is far from clear that these  dramatic changes will get past the parliamentary Labour Party or their activists. 

Thirdly, the idea that government needs to get in the way again. I say this partly tongue-in-cheek; there are lots of areas where government can better help young people, and his proposals around apprenticeships and mental health provision are sensible. 

Unintended consequences

There are also some areas where I am genuinely conflicted, especially over an increased employment support programme. Currently, only £1 is spent on employment support for every £25 spent on benefits. Milburn wants to get that ratio to £1 of support for every £2 of benefits – hopefully by reducing the bill as well as increasing support. The review proposes that young people should be given guarantees of employment. Much of the work would be assigned to Mayors who will be responsible for ensuring opportunities are available in their local areas. 

On the one hand, countries like the Netherlands with low NEET rates do have intensive and localised employment support – people literally knock on doors and get young people into work or training. It makes sense to learn from that. On the other hand, previous British attempts at employment programmes haven’t been especially successful in moving large numbers of people into work. I just don’t trust the British state’s ability to design and run programmes that will actually be cost-effective. 

But there are some areas where his proposals will cost money, introduce complexity and have unintended consequences. For example, his proposals to pay employers £3000 to take on young people who are NEET will increase complexity and bureaucracy. It means employers may not take on the best person for the job. Likewise, asking the government to hire more young people or include youth employment in procurement contracts also introduces more bureaucracy. We also need much more accountability from Mayors who are going to be responsible for improving employment outcomes.  

Overall, I want to applaud Milburn’s ambition. He is trying to solve a big problem that has an enormous fiscal, economic and moral cost. However, I am concerned about the politics. We know that this Labour Party is highly averse to welfare cuts and loves government intervention. There is a risk that patchy implementation of this review will leave us with the worst of all worlds – pushing ahead with the increased government intervention and subsidy, without addressing the core incentives in the welfare system and reducing regulatory costs and taxes for business.

Daniel Herring is head of economic & fiscal policy at the Centre for Policy Studies

YES: The Nvidia board stated they have no reason to believe any secrets were compromised

It also requires a commitment to transparency as the likely congressional investigation gets going. This is unlikely to be a short-lived process, but is the only way forward. Now it has to show that.

Chris Beauchamp is chief market analyst at IG Group

THE VERDICT

You may think being caught having an affair with a potential Chinese spy would be pretty hard to come back from, but stranger things have happened in Silicon Valley.

That over 8,700 of the campaign’s signatories come from Nvidia staff members themselves is also notable. Those 8,700 staff backers also come from a staff count of over 42,000, leaving more than 33,000 employees unaccounted for in whether they support Huang’s return.

Taking back an ex can be oh so tempting, but most of us know it’s never for the best.

Robert Pattinson will be a great Bond – but his casting is bad news for Hollywood and its diminishing reputation for turning out new leading men

In new stills released today it has been announced that Twilight and Batman actor Robert Pattinson will be the seventh actor to officially drink freezing cold vodka and a tiny bit of vermouth to play orphaned, traumatised, fashionable, perennially middle-aged James Bond.  

Pattinson, who is 40 and rose to prominence through the five filmic adaptations of the Twilight Saga books, is a good choice. Firstly, he is a fine actor, with a range of indie projects under his belt, and an undefinable, hard-to-read quality that makes him alluring to Hollywood. You couldn’t quite pinpoint where he hangs out – the pub, a fine pile in the Hollywood Hills or a grungy gig – and it is that indie-to-mainstream crossover appeal has helped him sustain a career this long, developing the sort of CV former 007 producer Barbara Broccoli prefers (Daniel Craig, too, had been an indie darling before he picked up the holster). 

If you were to rank his undefinable, draw-you-in qualities, those smokey eyes that somehow seem both blue and brown but give nothing away would be at the top of the list.

Robert Pattinson is good for James Bond, bad for Hollywood

But Pattinson’s casting is less good for Hollywood. James Bond is surely the last role that could rocket an unheard of actor to the A-List, and not casting a burgeoning name is a missed opportunity. 

These days, it is incredibly hard to birth new stars. It was not this way in the 1990s when Pierce Brosnan was cast, and to some extent with Daniel Craig. Back then, putting a new face on the cover of The Sunday Times Culture magazine could make someone famous. I recall the former editor of that magazine telling me he’d once argued to give the cover to a little-known actor called Tom Cruise, and we all know how that went. But journalism doesn’t have a tenth of that power anymore – put someone on the front of a weekend supplement and they might generate a few hundred Instagram followers, but not a glittering Blockbuster career.

And then there are the nepo babies – the Anais Gallaghers, Hero Fiennes Tiffins and Rafferty Laws – clogging up the talent pipeline, making it even harder for new actors who don’t have famous parents to break through. 

The cinema also used to be a good platform for rising actors, but with fewer people going to the flicks at the weekend, and fewer films being made, producers are choosing safety by relying on bankable stars rather than newcomers (hello, R Patz). The death of the rom-com is a signifier of how people are mostly going to the cinema to see ‘event’ films these days, like new Batman, Spider-Man or James Bond films.

The power of franchises at the box office was proven again recently when Tom Cruise’s latest film, Digger, became one of the biggest box office disasters of the decade. Cruise’s casting alone couldn’t drum up interest from the public, illustrating how big stars can’t always guarantee box office return without the weight of franchises like Mission Impossible behind them.

One man who can, though, is James Bond. Ian Fleming’s spy could remedy all of these problems: I’ll put it simply: cast anyone to play him, and the cinemas will sell out.

I mean, not literally anyone, but cast someone good, and people will go. 

This clearly doesn’t play into the interests of new Bond owners Amazon – they just want a big name because a big name sells, especially after investing £1bn in new Pinewood studio expansion.

Not that former producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G Wilson took this tack: when they cast a new actor as Bond, it was always a burgeoning name rather than an A-Lister. Daniel Craig had been in indie movies like Layer Cake; Timothy Dalton was more famous as a stage actor; Connery was a struggling working class actor from Scotland and Roger Moore a TV star rather than leading films. But look at the effect Bond had: Daniel Craig surely owes the critical success of his recent turns in Luca Guardagnino’s Queer and Knives Out to his role as 007.

Creating an exciting new star is high-on impossible these days – and Bond choosing not to take a punt on an upcoming name is a shame for Hollywood.

At a moment when travel feels like too much of an investment to waste on a one-note trip, South Africa makes a particularly strong case for itself. Few countries offer so much, so close together: safari, winelands, penguins, elephants, two oceans and one of Earth’s strangest botanical landscapes

To a vulture circling overhead, Earth Lodge is almost invisible. A short flight from Cape Town to Skukuza and a 45-minute drive through the savannah delivers you to almost nothing: just red dust, bleached grassland, and heat rising in waves from the ground. I’m led down a sloping cement tunnel and emerge into a cool, cave-like sanctuary. Water moves quietly over a natural rock pool, and beyond, an open wall frames immense, uninterrupted views of the Sabi Sabi Private Game Reserve.

This was once unbroken wilderness, a formidable stretch of bush deep in the Greater Kruger, close to the Mozambique border. One of the world’s great leopard strongholds, alive with traffic of the entire food chain, edged by the Sabie River, thick with crocodiles and hippos.

The ideal South Africa holiday itinerary

In 1979, South African investment banker Hilton Loon, and his wife Jacqui Loon opened their first lodge here and began building what would become one of Africa’s most enduring names in safari. Four decades, and four lodges later, Sabi Sabi has expanded westward to Cape Town, with the opening of The Claremont Boutique Hotel. It’s a natural evolution. South Africa defies a single landscape: to experience it fully is to move, within hours, from the shaded terraces of old wine country to the primal elegance of the bushveld.

Built at the turn of the millennium, Earth Lodge is no polished colonial fantasy. It has brutalist bones and recedes into the land with walls rendered from the very earth excavated to create them. Inside, felled trees are repurposed as furniture, with animal hide warming the slate and shadow. The 13 suites are palatial and private, though privacy is always relative at an unfenced lodge – a rustle outside is likely to have a heartbeat. Elephants saunter up to drink from the plunge pool, and skittish impala appear as I test the outdoor shower, prompting the peculiar, electric intimacy of holding another creature’s gaze.

The Big Five

We saw the Big Five within 24 hours. It was not my first safari, but it was my first leopard sighting: a female draped beneath a tree with the sort of molten-eyed disdain that would be intolerable in a person but magnificent in a leopard. After that came wildebeest, zebras, white rhinos, buffalo locking horns with graceless momentum, bashful warthogs bolting into the scrub, tails raised like little radio masts, and an elderly giraffe happily munching on acacia thorns. We returned daily to a coalition of lion brothers sprawled in the aftermath of a night’s hunting.

The advantage of a private reserve is the freedom to leave the marked tracks. But proximity is only half of it. The greater privilege is to have the bush translated for you. Louis, our tracker, grew up on the edge of this landscape and reads it with a sixth sense: a softened paw print, a snapped stem, a hint that something was here. He jumps down from the Land Cruiser carrying his stick, exchanging glances with Ranger Jamiel that seem to contain an entire silent language of trust. Louis heads off between burnt trees, while Jamiel drives on, providing the steady commentary of someone who’s seen this play out many times before. Moments later, we find her – a young lioness lounging in the dappled shade of a marula tree.

Their calm authority rests on deep foundations. Louis hails from a local Shangaan village and has spent decades at Sabi Sabi. The reserve’s relationship with the land is bound to the surrounding communities. Many of the staff are local, and the Sabi Sabi Foundation builds on that connection, investing in education, employment and conservation through projects including a Ranger Academy, alongside anti-poaching efforts that protect the wildlife everything here depends on.

Read more: Why South African wine is the GOAT

The spotted hyena

An hour before sunset, the 4×4 eases into a riverine thicket at the sight of elephants. A calf no bigger than a Labrador is tucked beneath her mother, slowly edging out to test the world with her trunk. We watch her in hushed fascination while Jamiel dismantles the half-baked myths we carry from childhood. The circle of life, it turns out, is not always a neat script of noble predators and hapless prey. No animal brings this home better than the safari’s most maligned criminal: the spotted hyena.

Far from a skulking scavenger, the hyena is in fact a matriarchal powerhouse. Females lead the hunt and outrank the males, with lions often opportunistic thieves stealing the hyena kills. I found them difficult to dislike, dog-curious and surprisingly tender, their rasping cackle a bonding call between friends. The Lion King owes several species a formal apology.

The reverse is equally true: Hippopotamuses, those watermelon-gobbling comedians, are among the deadliest and most territorial creatures in Africa. A young bull had recently defeated the dominant male and claimed lordship of the waterhole. His rival was a windfall for every carnivore within ten miles.

Read more: Inside South Africa’s two most exceptionally fabulous hotels

Hippo lore

Back at the lodge, hippo lore is shared over food. Tip of the day: if one charges, run in a zigzag line. Safari has a way of sharpening the appetite, and a breakfast of chakalaka, vibrant fruit, and omelettes generously loaded with biltong satisfies the ravenous elation that comes from three hours on open ground. By night, stories gather around the fire in the boma, a traditional circular enclosure historically used to protect livestock from predators, now ringed with lanterns and perfumed by smoky meats on the braai. Best of all are the sundowners, pulling over in the bush at sunset for drinks on foot. A glass of Amarula in hand, feet planted firmly on the same ground I’d seen a leopard pass that morning.

As soul-stirring as safari may be, Sabi Sabi’s newest opening suggests that it is only one facet of South Africa’s appeal. Rather than planting a flag in Cape Town’s obvious enclaves, they chose Claremont, a suburb bordering the Constantia valley, where some of the Southern Hemisphere’s oldest vineyards sit in an indecently green fold of land.

The Claremont Boutique Hotel opened in late 2025 with 15 rooms spread across a restored Cape Dutch revival manor, its gardens and pool. Built in 1928 by the pioneering female architect Magdalena Gertrude Sauer, it has a kind of romantic order that makes you feel like you’ve wandered into the house of somebody who inherited excellent taste. Veld & Vine does precisely what a suburban luxury hotel restaurant needs to do: keeps the day alive.

The bounty of South Africa

Expect excellent aged steaks, Durban bunny chows (curry-stuffed brioche, hello) and seafood from a nearby marine researcher-turned sustainable fisherman. But it is a base not a bubble, with easy access to Cafés and antique shops in Kalk Bay, once named the coolest neighbourhood in the world, and the penguin colony at Boulders Beach. Sabi guests can also book a wine safari at Klein Constantia’s iconic estate; a glass of Vin de Constance is a must. This modern revival of the sweet Muscat Constantia Wyn counted Dickens, Austen and Napoleon among its fans, the latter having thirty bottles a month shipped to St Helena during his exile.

Botanists use the term floral kingdom to describe the world’s six plant regions, categories that usually cover enormous tracts of the globe. The Cape Floral Kingdom occupies just the southwestern corner of the country but harbours an absurd concentration of life: species for species it’s fourteen times denser than the Amazon, and Table Mountain alone has more plant species than the entire UK. Head to Kirstenbosch to see these blooms in abundance. The wildlife there is no less eccentric.

In the end, my most starstruck moment was not with an apex predator, but what looked like a long-legged Furby hovering in a bush. I still have no idea what it was. Where are Jamiel and Louis when you need them?

The bank said demand for Nvidia’s chips continued to outstrip supply, although leadership uncertainty and tightening US export restrictions had increased risks to future growth.

Melissa Otto, global head of Visible Alpha Research at S&P Global, warned that Nvidia faced a crisis of investor confidence.

“There’s a complete evaporation of confidence at the moment, and there’s so much uncertainty around a lot of qualitative issues,” she said. “The narrative needs to come back to fundamentals. How is the business doing? Is it achieving what it said it’s going to achieve?”

Interim chief executive Colette Kress will lead Tuesday’s earnings call, with investors scrutinising fourth-quarter guidance, margins and whether Nvidia can maintain its ambitious longer-term growth forecasts.

China chip crackdown adds to Nvidia’s troubles

The results also come as Washington tightens restrictions on advanced AI chips reaching China through overseas data centres.

New US Commerce Department rules require licences for certain chip shipments to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil, potentially disrupting Nvidia’s international sales.

The measures follow scrutiny of Singapore-based Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer linked to Alice Huang, whose alleged Chinese intelligence connections helped trigger the leadership crisis.

The regulatory uncertainty comes amid wider concerns over the sustainability of Big Tech’s enormous AI infrastructure spending.

Danni Hewson, head of financial analysis at AJ Bell, warned that Huang’s departure could have consequences beyond Nvidia.

“Under Huang’s guidance, Nvidia spread its tentacles far and wide into the AI ecosystem,” she said. “If it loses momentum, many other interconnected companies could also find themselves held back.”

Alan Milburn’s review on youth joblessness has urged John Healey to find billions of pounds more in spending each year on young people in order to deliver projected savings in 10 years’ time. 

Milburn’s flagship report on helping Britain’s Neets, who are young people out of employment, education and training, has said that the government must allocate £5.8bn more in public funds each year on employment opportunities by 2036. 

The report said delivering new investment “should be a priority” in next year’s Spending Review, adding to a multitude of pressures facing the Chancellor around defence funding and public sector pay increases. 

Cuts to benefits of around £3.6bn are only set to come into effect from 2036, with initial savings on welfare largely to begin after the next General Election. 

Milburn said on Tuesday morning that the government could secure some savings if legislation is passed quickly through parliament as he said “crude cuts” would lead to “more poverty, more penury” as well as higher costs on crime and housing. 

In the short term, the government faces the task of finding about £500m in funding from existing departmental budgets for investment to enable under 25-year-olds to enter the national workforce. 

Analysis in the Milburn review suggested that cumulative welfare savings between 2030 and 2036 will add up to £13.7bn. Increased tax receipts from greater employment and a 0.4 percentage point addition to GDP each year could mean the Treasury yields a net saving, under Milburn’s projections. 

However, when new spending is accounted for, taxpayers are due to save just £200m a year after a decade of new changes. 

New problem for Spending Review

The government is due to respond to recommendations in a parliamentary statement this afternoon. 

Proposals in the report could set Healey up for a challenging Spending Review as the Chancellor refused to rule out further tax rises last week to deal with a growing list of demands on public finances. 

Government figures are also tasked with winning over Labour backbenchers to push through welfare reforms. Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, told MPs on Monday that the government had to “reset the system” and offer a “new settlement for young people”. 

The review also called for funding from the apprenticeship levy to be targeted as opportunities for young people. Mayors would also be accountable for delivering services that help under 25-year-old people into the world of work and also gain some of the benefits of welfare savings. 

Milburn puts spotlight on Labour’s taxes

The Blair-era health secretary’s core ambition was to reach ‘Neet zero’ in a decade’s time, bringing the rate down from a 13.4 per cent baseline to about five per cent. This would mean that 600,000 more young people were in work, education or training as currently nearly 1m people are Neets. 

An interim report in May found that the cost of the Neets crisis totalled about £125bn a year. For every £1 that was spent on employment or education opportunities, about £25 was spent on benefits. 

The report also noted the intergenerational gaps in public spending between children and pensioners, which had grown by about 170 per cent between 2004 and 2025. 

Reforms in the report include making mayors more accountable for getting young people into work, replacing the health element of Universal Credit with a new youth allowance scheme, adding mental health support and subsidising employers with a £3,000 payment if they take on Neets for at least 6 months. 

Milburn also recommended a “glide path” towards cutting employers’ National Insurance contributions by raising the threshold from £5,000 to £10,000 over several years “when fiscal conditions allow”. 

The initial cuts for employers hiring 21 to 24-year-olds should be targeted at the retail and hospitality sectors first, according to the former health secretary. 

His calls for a partial reveral of Rachel Reeves’ tax hikes bring the Labour government’s previous decisions under renewed scrutiny.

Helen Whately, the shadow work and pensions secretary, said: “Milburn is right to criticise the tax and regulation burdens Labour have imposed on businesses. But his review is too cautious on reversing that damage and too often his answer is the big and expensive hand of the state. 

“Overall, it fails to bring down the welfare bill, proposes billions more in government spending and won’t make the slightest difference for young people stuck on welfare now – because nothing will happen for at least three years.”

Former West Ham vice-chair Baroness Karren Brady has launched a new commercial agency for sport and entertainment with fellow former Hammers director Nathan Thompson.

Brady Thompson will focus on securing deals in sponsorship, improving hospitality and advising brands on strategy in order to tap “hundreds of millions of pounds in untapped commercial value”.

It comes seven months after Brady and Thompson departed West Ham, the former after 16 years running the club for owners and long-standing associates David Sullivan and the late David Gold.

“Sport and entertainment have never been more commercially powerful,” said Brady, whose profile has also been boosted by a long-running role on the BBC’s The Apprentice.

“Audiences are global, brands are increasingly recognising the value of being part of that world, and the commercial opportunities are enormous. Yet there remains a significant gap between the value organisations are currently generating and what they could achieve.

Brady Thompson’s decades of experience in sport

Brady, 57, has spent more than three decades in professional football, first at Birmingham City, where then-owners Gold and Sullivan named her managing director aged 23.

After they sold up and bought their childhood club West Ham, she followed them to east London and struck their low-cost 99-year deal to be anchor tenants of the former Olympic Stadium.

She stepped down in April, foreshadowing a period of turbulence at the club in which Sullivan resigned amid historic allegations, which he denies, and West Ham’s relegation from the Premier League.

Thompson, 43, spent 10 years in sales roles at West Ham, rising to the post of executive director, commercial, marketing, digital and content last year. Prior to that he had spells at Tottenham Hotspur and in sports advisory.

“I’ve sat in boardrooms on every side of these deals – as a sales executive, an adviser and a board member,” said Thompson.

Modella Capital has kicked off a sale of TG Jones, the high street business that formerly traded as WH Smith, less than two years into its ownership.

The private equity firm has called in advisors at Teneo to oversee an auction of the retail business, which includes about 350 shops and 3,500 workers, in the weeks running up to Christmas. 

Modella had not been proactively seeking a deal but decided to trigger an auction after receiving unsolicited expressions of interest in buying the business, it is understood.

The process will take place in the coming weeks, but a transaction would not take place until after Christmas, in the first quarter of next year, sources close to the matter told City AM.

The group snapped up WH Smith’s 480 high street shops for an initial £10m in June last year and later pushed through a divisive restructuring plan which it claimed was necessary to ensure the retailer’s survival. The turnaround plan, opposed by landlords who objected to proposals to slash the rent paid by TG Jones, triggered the closure of up to 150 of the retailer’s sites.

Modella faced criticism for its early stewardship of the former WH Smith shops, after it rebranded each site with new TG Jones branding and charged royalties for the new moniker.

The private equity firm believes it has set the retailer back on the right course since taking over, with one person close to Modella saying it is now a “viable but smaller” business.

Joe Price, Modella’s managing director, said: “When TG Jones was acquired in 2025, it was a loss-making business with an uncertain future. Turning it around meant taking some hard decisions, including closing stores through a court-approved restructuring plan. 

“We are extremely grateful to our colleagues from across the business for their continued support. The turnaround is starting to deliver, and we are seeing improved trading results,” he added.

TG Jones sale to shake up high street

The auction of TG Jones, first reported by Sky News, will inevitably draw comparisons with the ongoing sale of Poundland, which is racing to avoid collapse after its owners, Gordon Brothers, refused bids which would have kept the discount retailer afloat.

Modella Capital is conscious of the timing, sources close to the process said, though they insisted that TG Jones is in a different position. 

The sale of Poundland has centred on a £30m loan Gordon Brothers inherited when it bought the company, which the investment firm has insisted be repaid in full. No such financial instrument would play a part in TG Jones’s auction, it is understood. 

Before Modella Capital bought its 480 shops, WH Smith had traded on UK high streets for 233 years, after being established as a newsagent by Henry Walton Smith in 1792.

Modella Capital has garnered a reputation for picking up struggling high street retailers, often putting them into administration soon after buying them. 

Claire’s Accessories and The Original Factory Shop both collapsed earlier this year after being bought by the private equity firm, though Hobbycraft, which Modella also owns, has survived its own restructuring plan.

Alex Willson, TG Jones chief executive, said: “As ever, our focus is on providing a great experience for customers, especially with the critical Christmas period coming up. 

“We continue to execute our turnaround plan, which is improving our performance month by month. We’re grateful to our fantastic colleagues for their commitment; and to our suppliers, our owner and other stakeholders for their continued support,” he added.

Ikea has “abandoned” plans for a number of new stores in Britain and could slow its expansion in the country even further, owing to the “unprecedented” costs facing retailers.

David McCabe, chief executive of the flat-pack furniture seller’s UK and Ireland business, said the Swedish retailer is considering investing instead in European markets with lower taxes, following the government’s “missed opportunity” to back the sector at last month’s Budget.

The furniture group has long enchanted British shoppers with its maze-like layout and offering of Swedish meatballs and has moved into smaller city centre stores, including on London’s Oxford Street, in recent months in a bid to get closer to the high street. 

“But it is a fact that there have been planned investments that Ikea intended to make in the UK that have been abandoned due to the increases in costs that we face,” McCabe told City AM. 

“I will be working with the team to be as creative as we can to ensure that we do continue to invest and expand in the UK. But it is becoming harder, of that there is no doubt.

“If we’re not able to make these cases for sustainable investments in the UK, Ikea as a company, we will invest in other European countries. That is the reality.”

The huge size of Ikea stores means the retailer inevitably pays a large amount of property tax but McCabe said the company’s business rates bill is significantly higher than the equivalent tax in any of the other European countries in which it operates. 

The Ikea boss said his firm had been hoping that John Healey would take action at last month’s Budget to address “the unprecedented period of high costs and complexity” facing the UK’s retail sector. 

The Chancellor claimed he would freeze the business rates bills of all high street firms, but industry bosses pointed out that this tax is still set to rise in line with inflation, piling the sector with an extra £250m in costs next year.

“We do see that it was a missed opportunity to back retail under real pressure. I do hope that the Prime Minister and his team really do urgently recognise the importance of the retail sector, and work together with us,” McCabe said. 

Ikea slashes prices

He added that Ikea is “positive” about the UK and would be keen to revisit some of the projects it has been forced to shelve, but would not be able to do so unless Labour provides “a sustainable cost picture and an incentive to continue to grow in the UK”.

Ikea’s shift to scaled-down stores has been driven by the rising business rates burden facing retailers. The industry pays 20 per cent of these tax receipts despite making up only five per cent of the UK economy, according to the British Retail Consortium (BRC).

As well as moving closer to high streets, Ikea has aggressively cut prices in recent months. Across 425 products, including its Billy bookcase and Hemnes sofa, the retailer spent £54m reducing prices by an average of 20 per cent in August. The group is rolling out further price cuts across 1,000 products in the run-up to Christmas.

McCabe said: “I think it’s fair to say that people across the country are facing unprecedented pressure when it comes to cost of living. 

“For us, the more challenging it is for our customers, the harder we need to work to ensure that the products that we have are accessible for our customers.”

Ikea’s boss said he was “proud” the retailer managed to grow its sales in a year that “wasn’t easy when it comes to the retail environment”. The group’s takings rose by just 0.5 per cent to £2.26bn in the last year, despite total store visits rising by seven per cent.
