Praxis-1 learns how objects behave and how tasks unfold from large-scale video. | Source: Runway

Praxis-1 learns how objects behave and how tasks unfold from large-scale video, which gives it a head start on a new embodiment before fine-tuning on any hardware or domain-specific data, explained Runway. The company’s research has shown that web video matches teleoperated robot video as pre-training data for policy performance, which shifts the bottleneck on a capable policy to how much general video a model can learn from.

“The tasks vary with the robot. Noble Machines builds a legged humanoid for heavy industrial handling, and with them Praxis-1 picks up wooden planks, places them in containers and clears mixed piles into bins,” Chen said. “Standard Bots makes six-axis arms for factory work like machine tending and palletizing. Ultra builds and deploys dual-arm stations that pack orders in warehouses. A humanoid, a single arm, and a pair of arms are very different machines, and the same model drives all three.”

“With our partners, a single Praxis-1 checkpoint has adapted to a variety of embodiments with light fine-tuning, and with LoRA, you can adapt it to your own embodiment, cameras and tasks without retraining the full model,” said Runway. “Fine-tuned on Google’s RT-1 robot, which never appeared in its training data, Praxis-1 reaches 80.0% success on SimplerEnv, well above the original RT-1 policy at 52.4%.”

Submit your innovation now!

Why keep Praxis-1 open weight?

Runway has been committed to shipping Praxis-1 as an open weight model since its initial announcement. Open weights give hardware developers the flexibility to run, inspect, and adapt a world action model on their own terms, according to the New York-based company.

“At Runway, we believe that U.S. leadership in physical AI is critical,” Chen asserted. “Regaining our global lead in manufacturing, accelerating productivity across our economy, and securing ourselves and our allies will rely on this.”

“Achieving this will require a significant increase in investment across both hardware and software, but it will also require a level of interoperability and openness from American models that does not currently exist for physical use cases,” he said. “We view open world models as a compounding advantage that gives hardware developers flexibility and control they don’t currently have.”

After making Praxis-1 available to developers, Runway said it is focusing on scaling deployments.

“We want Praxis-1 in the real world: in real warehouses, factories, and industrial sites, doing real work,” Chen said. “We believe the frontier of robotics will be discovered through real-world applications, not in a lab. So what comes next is deploying with our partners, learning from what the model runs into out there, and putting those lessons back into the model.”

Berkeley says yes https://www.therobotreport.com/can-ai-agents-program-industrial-robots-without-training-data-berkeley-says-yes/ https://www.therobotreport.com/can-ai-agents-program-industrial-robots-without-training-data-berkeley-says-yes/#respond Wed, 11 Nov 2026 12:55:16 +0000 https://www.therobotreport.com/?p=590113 UC Berkeley and NVIDIA have released open-source tools for teams of AI coding agents that write, simulate, and refine readable robot programs. 

The post Can AI agents program industrial robots without training data? Berkeley says yes appeared first on The Robot Report.

]]>

The new RoboSimStudio is an open-source project that enables agentic AI coding of robotic simulation environments. | Credit: UC Berkeley

UC Berkeley and NVIDIA have released open-source tools for a new approach: enabling teams of AI coding agents to write, simulate, and refine readable robot programs.

Since the early days of industrial robots, programming, tuning, and troubleshooting robotic workcells has taken weeks to months. New research coming out of UC Berkeley has demonstrated that new agentic AI programming tools could change how industrial robots are coded and maintained.

Why is this important? As anyone who’s programmed an industrial workcell knows, implementing the code has to wait until the end of the design and fabrication process. The robot needs to be installed in the workcell; all of the feeders, conveyance, and other elements also need to be installed. The pressure to get this done all falls on the software team, often when the project deadline is looming.

The new toolset goes beyond the idea of “vibe coding” a robot application. While it generates code with large language models (LLMs), what’s novel is the use of AI agents to manage the coding, testing and deployment.

“Agentic robotics is a fundamental shift in how robots are programmed,” said Ken Goldberg, the William S. Floyd Jr. Distinguished Chair in Engineering at UC Berkeley. “Instead of collecting massive amounts of data and hand-tuning every behavior, teams of agents can quickly generate, test, and refine robot programs that allow human engineers to interpret how the programs work for fine-tuning and verification.”

Researchers introduce GaP and VABAR

  • Graph-as-Policy (GaP) is a modular framework that splits a task into skills — perception, grasp planning, collision-free motion — which agents generate, connect and rehearse in simulation.
  • Variational Automation Benchmark for Agentic Robotics (VABAR) is a benchmark of six tasks: tool sorting, tool hanging, gear meshing, syringe packing, cable insertion, and cable routing. It is built built on Isaac Lab-Arena and Newton, with standardized variations and difficulty tiers.
  • The UC Berkeley and NVIDIA team presented the concept at CoRL 2026 this week in Austin, Texas.

How the toolset works

Dr. Goldberg described the research to The Robot Report. In September, Eric Chen, one of his graduate students, give GPT-6 Astra Eric’s new RoboSimStudio tool to see if it could generate not just a graphic model, but also a full 3D simulation of a scene. And that’s exactly what happened.

According to Goldberg, Chen gave the model a video and this new tool, and within an hour, it had generated a Newton simulation that was incredibly similar to the video.

“When a new frontier model came out in early September, they gave it the tool and a video,” said Goldberg. “Within about an hour, it produced a Newton simulation closely matching the video, by iterative trial and error.”

“And Newton [simulation] is really wonderful,” he added. “The problem is Newton is very complicated. It has a lot of parameters, hundreds of parameters. So generally, people didn’t really use it that much because it’s just too complicated, too many dials and switches.”

Goldberg praised Chen for pulling this together. Initially, Chen built the tool just for himself.

“I want my student Eric to get credit for this,” he said. “He basically sat down and built a new interface for Newton called RoboSimStudio. It is basically just an interface that makes you have sliders on the right-hand side of your screen, and you have a visualizer on the left. … You can tune all these parameters much easier than you could before, so he built that just for himself to make the simulation part easier.”

But simulation alone isn’t enough, according to Goldberg. Simulation matters to the whole approach of using agents to code robots.

“The agent needs a simulator to be able to basically iterate and see how to improve this code,” he said. Goldberg noted that the existing tools “were not very reliable and had a lot of problems.”

The harness converts a VA task specification into a computation graph, optimizes it via self-learning in simulation, and hands G* to an edge-based interpreter that drives the robot — sim and real feedback close the loop. | Credit: UC Berkeley

Agents write and test code

Agentic robotics operates in a loop: Agents write robot code, test it in simulation, see where it fails, and revise. That loop is only as good as the simulator behind it.

Newton Physics, the open-source physics engine that UC Berkeley chose, is powerful but exposes hundreds of parameters, which has kept many developers from using it.

RoboSim Studio made those parameters tractable, and that turned the simulator from a bottleneck into something an AI agent could tune on its own.

UC Berkeley developed the VABAR benchmark suite with NVIDIA Isaac Lab-Arena open-source policy-evaluation framework and the Newton physics engine. It includes a detailed physics-based simulation for contact-rich robot-object interactions.

VABAR evaluates how robots perform on practical manipulation tasks ranging from tool sorting and handing to cable insertion and routing. The tool facilitates comparisons and measures progress across realistic industrial tasks, changing conditions, and increasing levels of difficulty.

Each task includes standardized variations, difficulty tiers, and success metrics, allowing researchers to measure progress, compare approaches, and evaluate whether systems can handle the demands of industrial operation. At the same time, Isaac Lab-Arena enables large-scale systematic evaluations across changing task conditions.

Spencer Huang, director of product for robotics at NVIDIA (and son of CEO Jensen Huang), has worked with Goldberg’s lab at UC Berkeley to interface with the NVIDIA product teams.

The partners listed some of the new capabilities:

  • Graph structure: Each node (perception, grasp, motion planning) can be assigned to its own agent, so agents work in parallel without “stepping on each other’s toes.”
  • ROS equivalence: The graph turns out to be equivalent to a ROS graph and can be converted to ROS 2.
  • Output: Python that calls existing vendor modules (such as KUKA) for low-level drive control. It does not replace robot controllers.
  • The harness: Thousands of prompts and structures constrain the agents.

How do agents change robot programming?

When asked how this new approach differs from straight “vibe coding” of an app, Goldberg responded that the magic is in the harness provided by GaP. The graph structure organizes the agents.

The code produced by “vibe coding” is already mature and well understood, he explained. The use of AI to write code is accepted in software engineering today. But rarely does an application function as intended in the first pass.

This is true for software from human engineers, and it’s equally true for software development developed with AI. Testing and iteration are needed to optimize the application, said Goldberg.

When applied to robotics, the best practice now is to test in simulation before deploying the code on a real robot. With agentic AI, a robotics engineer can enable the agent to iterate on both the simulation environment and then the subsequent code to more efficiently develop the robotic application.

For instance, Bosch is evaluating agentic robotics for diverse industrial automation scenarios. “Agentic robotics holds great promise because it generates interpretable code that engineers can thoroughly analyze before production deployment,” said Liu Ren, senior vice president and AI fellow at Bosch Research. “Bosch Research is actively collaborating with Goldberg and Huang and their teams.”

“AI-powered industrial robots must continuously improve reliability and performance,” said Jeff Mahler, co-founder and chief technology officer of Ambi Robotics. “Agentic robotics converted production data into robot behavior updates, increasing throughput across our U.S. fleet while keeping engineers in control.”

Goldberg is also an advisor to Ambi Robotics.

]]> Isomorphic Labs, an AI company focussed on designing and developing new medicines, today announced a €4.5 billion ($5 billion) Series C financing round to accelerate the scientific breakthroughs and proprietary AI advances.

The round was co-led by Greenoaks and Sequoia Capital, alongside Andreessen Horowitz, with continued significant investment from Alphabet. The round also included participation from all existing investors: Thrive Capital, MGX, GV, CapitalG, Temasek and the UK Sovereign AI Fund.

“When we founded Isomorphic, our conviction was that biology could be understood and modelled at the most fundamental molecular level and radically accelerated through AI,” says Sir Demis Hassabis, founder and CEO of Isomorphic Labs. “Our drug design engine is generating molecules with unprecedented precision and speed. This round enables us to accelerate our progress: building foundational biology models, deepening our systemic disease understanding, and driving our first therapeutic programs towards clinical trials to deliver tangible impact for patients.”

The announcement comes amid several other European investments in AI-enabled drug discovery and pharmaceutical research during 2026 – although nowhere near as large.

In the UK, London-based Helical raised €8.4 million for its virtual AI laboratory, Ternary Therapeutics secured €4.1 million for AI-designed molecular glues, and Sable Bio attracted €3.15 million for its drug-safety platform.

Elsewhere, France’s Orakl Oncology raised €30 million and Rivercell secured €22 million, while Switzerland’s Adaptyv Bio announced €34.35 million for automated biological testing.

Together with other relevant rounds involving WhiteLab Genomics, Generare and Sightera Biosciences, these financings represent approximately €148.2 million in 2026 funding reported by EU-Startups, excluding Isomorphic Labs.

EU-Startups also previously covered Isomorphic Labs’ €1.8 billion Series B among the major UK technology financings of the first half of 2026.

“Isomorphic Labs is building foundational technology for the future of medicine,” adds Konstantine Buhler, Partner at Sequoia Capital. “It’s inspiring to see the Isomorphic team translate advanced AI into a growing portfolio of drug candidates. Using AI to improve human health is one of the most important challenges of our generation. We’re proud to co-lead this round and help further scientific discovery in medicine.”

Isomorphic Labs was founded in 2021, the company has built a world-leading AI drug design engine comprising foundational AI models that are capable of working across multiple therapeutic areas and drug modalities.

Isomorphic is scaling its proprietary drug design engine (IsoDDE) and therapeutic candidate pipeline designed with AI to deliver the next generation of medicines. IsoDDE unifies a suite of foundational simulation AI models that natively work across multiple therapeutic areas and drug modalities.

IsoDDE explores vast chemical spaces to design, refine, and deliver engineered molecules with optimal drug-like properties.

The company outlines that the breadth and precision of the simulation models within IsoDDE push predictions towards experimental accuracy and provide a suite of capabilities to advance innovative medicines. Combined with powerful proprietary agents that navigate and reason over highly complex biological systems, these models directly and repeatedly translate into advancements across the company’s multi-modality pipeline of therapeutic candidates, addressing some of the most challenging problems in the industry.

“Every week we are making repeatable scientific advancements enabled by our models,” says Max Jaderberg, President of Isomorphic Labs. “These translate directly into better molecular profiles with the potential to be new medicines and unlock some of the hardest problems in drug discovery. Our interdisciplinary teams combine world-leading machine learning researchers with top-class drug hunters and together they are routinely solving complex biological problems that have stalled traditional research for decades.

“We are translating our discoveries directly into potential life-changing medicines, built on the infrastructure we are establishing for the future of bioengineering with this investor backing.”

Today’s capital will continue to mature IsoDDE as well as expand deeper into new biology with highly advanced models. To deliver new and transformative classes of therapeutics, Isomorphic is creating a partner ecosystem to advance the understanding of mechanistic disease biology. In parallel, the company is building the global infrastructure required to power the future of AI-led bioengineering.

Proceeds will also support the company’s continued build of scalable AI-first translational and clinical development infrastructure as it advances its drug candidates to clinical trials.

The post Opinion: Maintaining the open web is central to Europe’s AI sovereignty ambitions appeared first on EU-Startups.

]]> Europe’s ambitions for AI sovereignty depend on giving its startups the resources to succeed, innovate and compete with established companies. As it stands, the EU remains heavily reliant on digital technologies developed and managed from elsewhere, raising questions about its ability to control the systems underpinning its economy.  

In June this year, the European Commission unveiled its European Technological Sovereignty Package. This includes the Cloud and AI Development Act, which specifically aims to support the research, development and innovation of next-generation AI technologies, including frontier AI models.  

The Tech Sovereignty Package also aims to fast-track the implementation of the European Commission’s existing AI Continent Action Plan. This encompasses many areas that are central to the EU’s AI sovereignty ambitions, including physical infrastructure, talent development, and regulatory simplification. One of the most notable of these is access to large volumes of high-quality data, which the plan specifically highlights as a requirement for bolstering AI innovation. 

For European AI startups, publicly available web data is a valuable resource for training models and building services that rely on current information. Yet emerging licensing models that treat public data as exclusive, regulatory uncertainties and restrictions on automated access risk putting that resource beyond the reach of smaller developers. Maintaining responsible access to the open web is therefore central to enabling businesses of all sizes to contribute to the EU’s AI sovereignty ambitions.  

AI sovereignty depends on an open web 

The internet itself was built on the principle that information can be published and accessed widely, without any one company controlling access to it. Within a few years of launching the World Wide Web, CERN placed the software in the public domain for anyone to use, modify and distribute. This openness allowed businesses, researchers and developers to build on shared foundations without seeking permission from a single technology provider.  

This principle underpinned, and continues to support, both the development and functioning of frontier AI systems. Varied public web data can help reduce gaps and biases in training data, helping AI models to deliver accurate, unbiased outputs. The rise of agentic AI has further increased the importance of access to public web data. It is being deployed across a growing range of services, from personal shopping and travel assistants to business research and IT support. 

Microsoft’s Work Trend annual index report found a 15-fold increase in active agents across its Microsoft 365 ecosystem between March 2025 and March 2026. For agents carrying out tasks on the web, however, restrictions on access to current information can limit their effectiveness. For example, an agent comparing suppliers or booking travel needs to check changing prices, availability and terms before acting. 

In October, research found that roughly a third of the several hundred leading US commerce, travel and reservation websites it tested blocked Meta’s Muse agent, while another third challenged or restricted its access. The biggest problem here is not for Meta, who have been negotiating leverage and large financial resources for legal disputes, but many smaller agent developers do not.

This limits their ability to innovate, as their agents have less access to up-to-date information. Consumers also lose out, with fewer competing services to choose from and agents that may be unable to compare the full range of products, prices and offers available. 

Such arbitrary restrictions threaten the EU’s AI ambitions as its AI startups are excluded from the market by the decisions of competing private companies. They also raise questions about consumer sovereignty in the free market and how it may be limited. 

While regulators discuss opt-outs, blanket blocks are implemented 

In September 2026, the European Commission launched a consultation on whether the EU’s copyright framework needs additional measures, including those addressing the use of copyright-protected content in AI. The resulting policy decisions could have significant implications far beyond AI.  

A key risk is that overly broad measures have unintended consequences as data resources previously used for innovation and value creation become virtually useless for society. They become exclusive to the biggest market players. For European startups, this translates directly into a competitive disadvantage against companies operating under more proportionate regulatory regimes. 

While the EU is still considering the scope of copyright holders’ opt-outs and how they should work, private companies are already implementing their own mechanisms, waiting neither for regulation nor for the website owner to actually make the choice. ​​If web hosts and platforms get to make such decisions instead of the users that created the content or the websites that published it, copyright will slowly lose its meaning.  

This will not be because of AI companies accessing content but because of the lack of control publishers will have over who can access their content. Both AI companies and publishers are seeking clarity over who can access content, for what purposes and on whose terms. These questions should be resolved through clear rules that give rights holders meaningful control, preserve lawful access to public web data and hold those who misuse it accountable. 

The web must remain open. This means lawful information published openly on the web should remain accessible. Personal, private information should remain protected, while the collection and use of personal data must comply with data-protection laws. And this is where the issue lies. We need to clearly distinguish what information is public and what information is deemed private.  

Beyond these regulatory questions, the risk for EU startups is the creation of a pay-to-play economy that favours large technology companies and well-financed incumbents with negotiated access to public data. This raises the cost of innovation and restricts European startups’ ability to catch up and compete, undermining the EU’s AI sovereignty ambitions. 

Enabling the EU’s AI sovereignty ambitions 

Creating a commercial and regulatory environment that supports innovation and global competitiveness is central to developing the EU’s sovereign AI ecosystem. Existing regulations and ongoing policy initiatives such as the AI Act provide an important foundation, but further work is needed to clarify compliance requirements and address barriers that favour well-financed incumbents.  

Access to the same publicly available information should not depend solely on a company’s financial resources or its ability to negotiate preferential deals. The EU needs to balance legitimate access to public web data with the protection of copyright and platforms’ commercial interests. These objectives can coexist, but developers and publishers need clearer rules about what information can be collected, for which purposes and under what conditions. 

Ultimately, the EU’s AI sovereignty ambitions depend not only on investment in infrastructure and talent but also on European companies’ ability to access and use diverse, up-to-date data.

]]> What if the supposed tradeoff between commercial success and positive impact was not an unavoidable reality of business, but a problem of business design? 

That is the central argument behind Impact Unleashed: Building Companies that Scale Positive Change, the new book by Jack Mardack, co-founder of global employment platform Oyster. 

Drawing on his experience building one of the few companies to achieve both unicorn status and B Corp certification, Mardack challenges a longstanding assumption in entrepreneurship: that founders must choose between commercial success and making a meaningful difference in the world. 

Instead, he argues that businesses can be designed so that growth and positive impact reinforce one another. 

The principle is captured in the book’s central idea: “impact by design, not by intention.“

Rethinking the relationship between profit and purpose 

For many companies, impact begins with good intentions. 

A founder builds a business, attracts customers and pursues growth. As the company becomes established, it may introduce sustainability commitments or corporate responsibility programmes designed to give something back. 

Mardack sees a weakness in that approach. When impact depends primarily on a company’s commitment to doing good, it can become vulnerable to competing demands around profitability and investor expectations. 

Impact Unleashed proposes a different starting point: what if the mechanism that generates revenue is also the mechanism that creates positive change? 

In this model, impact is not something a company must continuously justify against commercial priorities. It is built into the way the company creates value. Rather than simply asking what problem their product solves and how the business will scale, Mardack encourages founders to consider what positive change their company could create, who would benefit and how that impact could grow alongside revenue. 

Mardack offers a simple diagnostic, which he calls the automaticity test: does the impact metric move automatically and proportionally with the commercial one? If it does, impact is designed in. If it depends on a separate decision, it is still only intended. 

The fourth ring of entrepreneurship 

One of the ideas Mardack explores is what he calls the fourth ring of entrepreneurship. 

In a previous interview, he describes the first three rings as familiar stages of entrepreneurial value creation: creating a job for yourself, creating employment for others and delivering value to customers. Each of these rings matters, and each is a real achievement. But founders are usually expected to think only as far as the third. For Mardack, the fourth ring is both a revelation and a new design challenge. 

The fourth ring is about creating measurable, structural positive impact through the business itself. This reframes entrepreneurial success. A company is no longer defined only by its revenue, jobs or customers, but also by the wider change its business model makes possible. 

Rather than viewing positive impact as a limitation on commercial ambition, the fourth ring encourages founders to see social and environmental challenges as opportunities to build businesses capable of delivering value and change at scale. 

Why good intentions and ESG scores are not enough 

Mardack’s argument comes as the business world’s approach to measuring responsibility and impact faces growing scrutiny. 

Environmental, social and governance (ESG) frameworks have long provided companies and investors with a common language for assessing corporate behaviour. But Mardack sees limitations in relying on standardised scorecards to capture the actual impact of individual businesses. 

According to Mardack, a software company and an ice cream company may be assessed against similar ESG criteria, despite having fundamentally different business models and opportunities to create positive change. 

While environmental performance, labour practices and governance remain important, those measures do not necessarily explain what a company’s core business contributes to the world. 

For Mardack, the next step is to develop an impact thesis: a clear explanation of how a business creates positive change, supported by evidence that the change is actually happening. 

Impact Unleashed explores how founders can develop an Impact Thesis, connect it to their business model and measure its effectiveness with enough rigour to withstand scrutiny from investors and other stakeholders. 

The distinction is between claiming to be a responsible company and demonstrating how commercial success produces meaningful outcomes. 

Lessons from building an impact-driven unicorn 

Mardack’s ideas are rooted in his experience co-founding Oyster, a global employment platform designed to expand access to international job opportunities. 

By connecting businesses with talent across borders, Oyster embedded positive impact into its business model, achieving both unicorn status and B Corp certification. 

As Mardack’s role evolved from CMO to Chief Impact Officer, Oyster approached impact reporting not as a compliance exercise but as an active pursuit of evidence: a standing effort to find out what the business was actually changing in the world. That pursuit led to a finding the company hadn’t set out to look for: Oyster was changing the lives of women globally in ways it had never specifically designed for. It is a discovery a rote, once-a-year report would likely have missed, and it shaped the practical frameworks in Impact Unleashed. 

Bringing the conversation to Europe’s founders 

The ideas in Impact Unleashed also raise questions about Europe’s entrepreneurial future. 

While Europe’s startup ecosystem is frequently judged against the United States on technology scale and venture capital, impact entrepreneurship offers another perspective on the continent’s potential. 

Mardack points to Europe’s long social-market tradition, still embedded in its culture and its laws. A better test of the continent’s potential, he argues, may not be where its trillion-dollar companies are, but whether Europe can show what is not yet happening at scale in the United States: companies genuinely thriving and creating value on the strength of their commitments to impact. That is how European founders could leapfrog the US model, rather than chase it. 

What if Europe’s opportunity is not simply to replicate Silicon Valley, but to develop globally ambitious companies with measurable positive impact built into their foundations? 

These themes will be explored at the MeOut Summit in Budapest on 25-26 November 2026, where Mardack will join Gábor Lévai, co-founder of Scale Impact, Hungary’s first B Corp, for a fireside conversation entitled “CEE’s Impact Moment.”

The discussion will examine Europe’s position in the global impact economy and whether Central and Eastern Europe can play a greater role in shaping the next generation of impact-driven businesses. 

Ultimately, Mardack’s question extends beyond any one company or region: what becomes possible when businesses are designed from the beginning to make money and make a difference through the same activity? 

Discover Jack Mardack’s book, Impact Unleashed, and explore the MeOut Summit agenda to join the conversation in Budapest.

]]> Copenhagen-based BioTech startup Commit Biologics has raised €54 million ($60 million) in Seed funding to develop new treatments for cancer and autoimmune diseases. The investment will help the Danish company bring its first drug candidate closer to clinical trials.

The final close was led by Ackermans & van Haaren, with participation from additional new investors AbbVie Ventures and M Ventures, and existing investors Bioqube Ventures, Korys and Novo Holdings.

“Commit was founded on a simple idea: that complement, one of the most powerful parts of our immune system, could be deliberately directed against diseased cells. With this financing, we will take COM002, a first-in-class immune engager that works independently of T cells, into the clinic and build the foundation for complement-powered immune engagers to become a new pillar of immunotherapy,” says Dr. Thomas L. F. Montgomery Andresen, CEO of Commit Biologics.

He adds: “Seeing our first development candidate backed by such a strong group of financial and strategic investors is a proud moment for the whole team.”

Commit’s financing comes amid several European immunotherapy and therapeutics investments reported in 2026.

In Switzerland, Nouscom secured €120 million for cancer immunotherapy development, while France’s ErVimmune and Brenus Pharma raised €17 million and €11 million, respectively, to advance their oncology programmes. In the Netherlands, Laigo Bio added €5.5 million for targeted cancer and autoimmune therapies.

Closer to home, Danish biopharmaceutical company Breye Therapeutics secured €67.5 million in a round co-led by Novo Holdings, while antibody-based cancer therapy developer PanTarg received a €1.3 million convertible loan.

These European therapeutics financing announcements in 2026 total approximately €278.5 million.

EU-Startups previously featured Commit Biologics in 2024 among ten European startups developing approaches to cancer treatment.

Charlotte Kremers, Principal at M Ventures, says: “Complement is among the immune system’s most potent effector mechanisms yet remains largely untapped in drug development. Commit has made it programmable in a standard antibody, creating a path to medicines with differentiated efficacy and safety profiles across indications.”

Founded in Copenhagen in 2021, Commit Biologics is creating a new drug category in immunotherapy by harnessing one of the immune system’s most ancient and powerful effector functions: complement.

Their proprietary Bispecific Complement Engager (BiCE) platform creates complement-powered immune engagers designed to selectively eliminate diseased cells. By recruiting C1q directly to malignant or pathological cells, BiCE antibodies activate complement precisely where it is needed, driving rapid and potent killing through a mechanism that does not rely on T cells.

Building on three decades of complement research at Aarhus University, they have spent years learning how to design effective complement-powered immune engagers. That work produced the BiCE platform and, more recently, their first drug candidate, which is now heading to the clinic.

The company expects complement-powered immune engagers to become a new pillar of immunotherapy, alongside T cell engagers and cell therapies.

Lenny Van Steenhuyse, Investment Manager at Ackermans & van Haaren, adds: “We firmly believe that Commit’s novel drug platform has the potential to generate a new treatment paradigm in immunotherapy based on the highly compelling preclinical data in targeted cell depletion. Ackermans & van Haaren is proud to support the Commit team and lead this financing to realise the full potential of the BiCE platform.”

Proceeds from the financing will support the completion of IND-enabling activities and IND filing for COM002, Commit’s first development candidate, which was announced last week.

COM002 is a dual-targeting BiCE molecule designed for targeted immune cell depletion, developed for patients with cancer and autoimmune disease. Additionally, the financing will advance a second programme into IND-enabling development and expand Commit’s BiCE pipeline.

]]> Treat, a Helsinki-based HealthTech startup co-founded by Swappie co-founder Sami Marttinen, has raised €3 million in a pre-Seed funding round.

The round was led by byFounders, an early backer of Lovable, alongside Illusian, the investment vehicle of Supercell founder Ilkka Paananen.

“Private healthcare across the globe is bogged down by fragmented systems and mismatched Incentives. Treat fixes this at the root. By stripping away billable runarounds and aligning technology directly with clinical workflows, the team behind Treat is building a new benchmark for primary care,” said Sara Rywe, General Partner at byFounders.

Founded in 2026 by Marttinen, former CEO of Finnish recommerce giant Swappie, alongside medical doctor Antti Mauno and FinTech engineering lead Onni Wahlberg, Treat is building an AI-native platform that connects patients with fully briefed doctors in minutes, eliminating the repeat visits and fragmented incentives that plague conventional private care.

The platform acts as a gateway to care, with patients first describing their symptoms in their own words via a chat interface, and an AI-powered intake tool structures the information into a detailed brief. A licensed physician registered with the Finnish Supervisory Agency (Lupa- ja valvontavirasto), not an algorithm, then reviews the case, makes every clinical decision, and either resolves it or routes the patient directly to appropriate follow-up care.

“As a doctor, I’ve seen how much time is lost before a patient gets to the right next step. We’re building Treat to remove that delay while equipping doctors with the best possible setup to help their patients,” said Mauno, medical co-founder, Treat.

Treat says its AI does not diagnose, assess urgency, or make automated decisions but only acts as an entry point of care. All patient data stays within the European Economic Area and is never used to train AI models.

While Treat is available directly to consumers at €72 per consultation, the company primarily focuses on employers. The platform is offered as a workplace health benefit, complementing existing occupational healthcare and private insurance rather than replacing them. With Treat, employers gain a tool that cuts unnecessary sick-day costs and removes the obstacle associated with seeing a healthcare professional without giving them access to individual health data. Employees, on the other hand, get immediate access to a fully briefed doctor without navigating complex healthcare systems.

Its revenue model is also fundamentally different from traditional private healthcare. Rather than profiting from the volume of appointments, referrals, or lab tests, Treat earns revenue only when a patient’s concern is genuinely resolved. According to the company, 62% of cases are resolved without any further appointment, with the median time to a doctor’s review at just 2 minutes and 14 seconds during service hours.

“Three years ago, my wife had to go through nine repeat doctor visits in private care before receiving a diagnosis. All the necessary information existed, but nobody had the incentive to connect the dots. The problem isn’t the doctors. It’s an economic model that rewards repeat visits over efficient resolution. Treat makes zero revenue from lab tests, clinic visits, or referrals. Our only incentive is solving the patient’s issue on the spot,” said Marttinen, co-founder and CEO of Treat.

]]> RHISE AI Technologies, the Munich-based startup behind Lucie, a personal AI designed for Europe, has raised an angel round of €2.66 million (just under $3 million, or $2.925 million to be exact).

The angel round saw participation from more than 40 investors, including Andy Bechtolsheim, co-founder of Arista Networks and the first outside investor in Google; Prince Max von und zu Liechtenstein, CEO of LGT; Dr. Klaus Kleinfeld, former CEO of Siemens, Alcoa and NEOM; Michael Baum, founding CEO of Splunk; Raoul Heraeus, managing partner of ALERA Capital; Leon Goretzka, former Germany international and Champions League winner; and European unicorn founders Jonas Rieke of Personio and Dr. Fabian Heilemann of Forto.

“European society deserves sovereign AI that serves people and does not consume them,” said Prince Max von und zu Liechtenstein, CEO of LGT.

Incorporated as a Delaware C-corp, RHISE AI was founded by Andy Loy, Danil Gontovnik, Samy Samandjeu, and Chris Seybold. Loy previously co-founded the industrial AI firm KONUX and scaled it to a valuation of around €693 million. He is also a former member of the World Economic Forum’s Global AI Council and a founding member of KI Bundesverband, Germany’s AI association. Gontovnik is a former Meta engineer who previously co-founded Anima AI and Noji, both of which were acquired.

The company builds a personal AI called Lucie, an idea shaped by Loy’s personal experience. In January 2021, the same month KONUX closed its oversubscribed Series C, Loy was hospitalised at 29. Becoming a father soon made him fixated on one question: why does the most powerful technology ever made compete for our attention instead of giving it back? He built RHISE AI and Lucie to answer it.

Designed for Europe, Lucie connects health, work, and personal data from wearables to calendars and inboxes and uses an in-house multi-agent system called Heartbeat to surface what needs attention without waiting to be asked. It can flag an unusually high bill, suggest a next step, and act once the user approves.

“Heartbeat sees what no single app can see: a short night before a packed morning, a promise buried in an email, a birthday you care about. Lucie suggests what to do, and nothing happens without your say. It has even found money people were owed and claimed it back for them. What people get back is time and attention for what really matters in life,” said Gontovnik, co-founder and CTO of RHISE AI.

The company stores personal data on sovereign European cloud infrastructure in Germany, operates under GDPR from day one, runs no advertising, and does not sell user data. Available for iPhone and Mac in English and German, Lucie has crossed more than 15,000 downloads in just over six weeks, with paid subscriptions priced at around €91 ($99.99) annually expected to exceed one thousand by year-end.

RHISE AI says more than half of active Lucie users have connected live health data from a wearable, which is in stark contrast to the 7% of US adults who say they are willing to share their health data with tech companies, according to Rock Health’s 2023 survey.

Personal AI and persistent AI agents have become the next frontier for tech companies, with Apple expanding the capabilities of Siri AI, Meta’s Muse topping app charts in the US, and OpenAI entering the segment with Dots. However, Siri AI and Meta Muse remain unavailable in the EU, while Google’s Gemini Spark excludes the European Economic Area. With 72% of Germans telling Bitkom in April 2026 that Germany is too dependent on the US for AI, RHISE AI wants to close the gap with Lucie.

“Personal AI will soon know more about us than any technology before it. The question is who it works for, Most of it is being built to capture attention. Everyone in this round has built something that lasted, and everyone in it wants Europe to build this category, not rent it,” said Loy, co-founder and CEO of RHISE AI.

The company says it measures impact not by engagement metrics but by hours given back to users, health goals reached and the carbon footprint of each AI conversation. Personal AI is set to become the next major interface following the PC, the web, and the smartphone, but most agents do their best work by harvesting user attention, and RHISE AI argues that the same intelligence can instead be redirected to restore it.

While AI agents have already demonstrated their ability to do repetitive tasks and give back valuable time, doing so within the confines of GDPR and the EU AI Act will be the real challenge for RHISE AI.

]]> Alecto, a British AI-native law firm, has raised a €18 million ($20 million) Seed round, to support the company’s expansion into additional areas of consumer law and new geographies, with its first international launch planned for 2027.

The round was led by Insight Partners, with participation from Firstminute Capital, Blue Lion Global, Andrena Ventures, FJ Labs, Antiportfolio Ventures, the Rigby Group, and Mishcon de Reya LLP, alongside angel investors Simon Rogerson (Octopus Group), and Jon Reynolds (SwiftKey).

Also in the UK, Keith raised €2.3 million to launch an AI-native law firm initially focused on conveyancing.

“Will brings deep knowledge of the property market to bear and the team’s progress in such a short timeframe clearly demonstrates the pace of execution. We’re very excited to be supporting Alecto and its next phase of growth.”

The team has grown from three people in January 2026 to 85 today, with over 500 years of collective legal experience between them.

According to the company, traditional legal services are attention-constrained: a finite number of qualified lawyers with limited hours each day. The status quo reflects an imbalance of supply and demand, with billing based on input, not outcomes, and a service model built around the lawyer’s needs, not the customer’s.

For consumers, this can mean high, often unpredictable costs, opaque processes, slow responses, and unfamiliar industry language that makes it hard to understand their options.

Alecto is building a service that moves matters forward proactively and explains legal issues in plain language, helping customers make informed decisions. Initially focused on the €2.9 billion ($3.3 billion) UK conveyancing market, the company aims to become the UK’s leading provider of property legal services in 2027.

Will adds: “Property is where we prove the model. We’re building the technology and operations to rapidly break into new countries and new areas of law. Ultimately, access to exceptional legal support should not depend on how much money you have or how confidently you can navigate the system.”

AGN https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/ Aerospace Global News Tue, 17 Nov 2026 15:30:44 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.4 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/cropped-AGN_Icon_Jet-32x32.png AGN https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/ 32 32 ICEYE unveils Gen5, the sharpest commercially built SAR satellite, with 11cm resolution https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/iceye-unveils-gen5-sar-satellite-onboard-ai/ Tue, 17 Nov 2026 16:38:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=56963 Finnish satellite manufacturer ICEYE has introduced Gen5, its fifth-generation synthetic aperture radar (SAR) spacecraft. Capable of 11cm resolution, doubled imaging capacity, and onboard AI processing, the platform is built to accelerate space-based intelligence for defence, government, and commercial operators.

The post ICEYE unveils Gen5, the sharpest commercially built SAR satellite, with 11cm resolution appeared first on AGN.

]]> Finnish satellite manufacturer ICEYE has unveiled Gen5, its most advanced synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellite yet, capable of capturing images with a resolution as fine as 11 centimetres, doubling imaging capacity and using onboard artificial intelligence to deliver critical information faster.

Announced on 16 November, the fifth-generation satellite is designed to provide governments, military operators and commercial customers with more detailed images, faster data delivery and the ability to monitor changes on the ground regardless of weather or daylight.

ICEYE describes Gen5 as the sharpest commercially built SAR satellite to date. Its highest-resolution mode, available to government customers subject to International Telecommunication Union (ITU) regulations, uses 1,800 MHz of imaging bandwidth to achieve the claimed 11cm resolution.

Commercial customers can access imagery with resolution as fine as 16cm using 1,200 MHz bandwidth.

The announcement comes amid growing demand for satellite-based intelligence and heightened concern about the security of spacecraft in low Earth orbit. ICEYE itself was involved in a closely watched orbital encounter last month when a Russian satellite approached one of its radar-imaging spacecraft.

Unlike conventional Earth observation satellites, which rely on reflected sunlight, SAR spacecraft transmit radar signals towards Earth and measure the returning echoes. This allows them to image the surface at night and through cloud cover, smoke and adverse weather.

The technology is particularly useful for tracking military deployments, monitoring maritime activity, detecting changes at strategic installations and assessing damage following natural disasters.

Gen5 doubles imaging capacity and improves ground resolution

The new satellite offers several improvements over ICEYE’s earlier generations, particularly in the number of targets it can observe during a single orbital pass.

According to the company, Gen5 reduces the minimum separation between consecutive imaging windows by more than 30%, allowing it to capture targets positioned closer together along its orbital path.

It also provides twice the imaging time per orbit compared with previous ICEYE satellites.

The company says these improvements allow approximately 30% more images to be collected during each pass, increasing the amount of intelligence that can be obtained without adding more spacecraft.

Gen5 can acquire more than 18 images in a multi-image acquisition sequence.

Its imaging modes range from broad-area surveillance covering up to 120,000 square kilometres to detailed observation of individual locations within a 5km by 5km scene.

The highest advertised resolution is achieved at a radar incidence angle of 50 degrees. At 30 degrees, ICEYE specifies a ground resolution of 17cm, subject to ITU regulations.

These capabilities would allow analysts to examine smaller objects and identify changes that might not be visible in lower-resolution imagery.

Gen5 is designed to operate at altitudes between 450km and 600km.

Improved orbital control will allow the satellite to follow repeatable ground tracks, passing over the same location from approximately the same viewing angle on successive observations.

That consistency matters when comparing images taken on different days. Changes in the position of vehicles, equipment, vessels or infrastructure can be easier to distinguish when the viewing geometry remains similar.

ICEYE also says the spacecraft can raise its orbit more quickly after deployment, reducing the time spent reaching its intended operating position.

Artificial intelligence moves onto the satellite

Another major development is the introduction of an onboard AI processor.

Traditionally, Earth observation satellites collect imagery and transmit it to ground stations, where computers and analysts process the information.

Gen5 is designed to begin some of that work in orbit.

Its AI processor will support future capabilities including image screening, preliminary processing, autonomous object detection and classification.

The system is also intended to support tip-and-cue operations, in which the detection of an object or activity can help direct further observation.

ICEYE stressed that these AI capabilities will be introduced progressively through software updates rather than being fully available from launch.

The satellite runs on the company’s IceOS software platform, allowing new functions to be uploaded after deployment.

Data transmission has also been improved. Gen5 supports downlink speeds of up to 1 gigabit per second using a steerable antenna, twice the speed of its previous generation.

Rafal Modrzewski, ICEYE’s chief executive and co-founder, said faster intelligence delivery was central to the new design.

“Time to decision is everything in space-based intelligence, whether you’re tracking a vessel or responding to a flood. Gen5 shortens it at every step: sharper and more images per pass, and AI analysis that starts in orbit.”

He added: “With a new generation approximately every 18 months and new software releases every quarter, our customers’ systems keep gaining capability.”

Russian satellite encounter raises security concerns

The Gen5 announcement follows an incident in October involving Russia’s Kosmos-2612 satellite and ICEYE-X36, which drew attention from independent satellite trackers and commercial space surveillance companies.

As previously reported by Aerospace Global News, orbital observations between 15 and 19 October showed Kosmos-2612 approaching the ICEYE spacecraft in low Earth orbit.

Satellite tracking specialist Marco Langbroek, whose Sattrackcam observations helped document the encounter, reported close approaches estimated at approximately one to two kilometres, with some calculations suggesting the spacecraft may have passed considerably closer.

Commercial satellite imagery from Vantor, captured on 17 October, also documented the proximity of the two spacecraft, with an estimated separation of around one kilometre.

LeoLabs subsequently reported that the Russian spacecraft was drifting away from ICEYE-X36 by 18 October.

The observations raised questions about the purpose of the Russian satellite’s manoeuvres, although the available evidence did not establish that it intended to damage or interfere with the ICEYE spacecraft.

The encounter was significant because ICEYE operates a commercial radar-imaging constellation whose data can support military intelligence and surveillance.

Russia has previously demonstrated an interest in rendezvous and proximity operations involving satellites, activities that can serve legitimate inspection purposes but can also raise security concerns when conducted near another operator’s spacecraft without coordination.

There is no indication that the October encounter directly influenced Gen5’s development or announcement.

However, it illustrates the increasingly contested environment in which commercial Earth observation companies operate, particularly when their imagery supports defence and intelligence missions.

ICEYE offers governments their own satellite constellations

Beyond improved image quality, ICEYE is positioning Gen5 as a complete intelligence system that governments can operate independently.

The company says a sovereign Gen5 capability can be delivered within 12 months of contract signature, including satellites, ground infrastructure, software and operator training.

The system is described as ITAR-free, meaning it is not subject to US International Traffic in Arms Regulations.

Existing ICEYE customers can integrate Gen5 satellites into their current infrastructure without replacing ground systems or changing established satellite-tasking procedures.

This compatibility is important for governments seeking to expand surveillance capabilities without developing an entirely new operating system.

ICEYE, founded in Finland, has built a substantial commercial SAR constellation serving defence, intelligence, environmental monitoring, insurance and emergency management customers.

Its satellites are used for applications ranging from monitoring military activity to assessing flood damage and detecting changes in critical infrastructure.

Gen5 is the company’s fifth satellite generation in eight years, reflecting its strategy of introducing new hardware approximately every 18 months while continuing to upgrade spacecraft already in orbit.

ICEYE has not specified a launch date for the first Gen5 satellite in its announcement.

The new platform is intended to strengthen the company’s position in a market where governments increasingly want frequent, high-resolution satellite imagery without depending entirely on traditional national reconnaissance systems.

]]> Just four months after the last Farnborough International Airshow (FIA), organisers have revealed that 93% of exhibition and chalet space for the 2028 event has already been sold or reserved.

The level of demand puts the UK airshow on course for the earliest sell-out in its 78-year history, with organisers adding another 1,900 square metres of exhibition space.

Further expansion is also being considered, following the introduction of a sixth exhibition hall and additional chalet facilities for the sold-out 2026 event.

When is the next Farnborough International Airshow?

The next FIA will take place from 17-21 July 2028, bringing together leading manufacturers, airlines, defence contractors and aerospace technology companies from around the world.

Why is Farnborough Airshow 2028 filling up so quickly?

The surge in bookings follows a record-breaking 2026 show, which welcomed 141,580 visitors – an increase of 41% compared to the 2024 airshow.

The five-day event generated more than $84.7 billion in commercial deals, including 353 firm aircraft orders and 904 firm engine orders.

As Aerospace Global News reported, Boeing emerged ahead of Airbus in the commercial aircraft order race, securing 186 firm orders compared with its European rival’s 157.

Major announcements also came from Embraer, GE Aerospace and Pratt & Whitney.

Aircraft orders were only part of the story: Farnborough also showcased developments in military aviation, autonomous systems and electric aircraft – including a public eVTOL transition flight by Vertical Aerospace.

Global aerospace companies have a major presence at Farnborough

Although held in the UK, Farnborough has become an important international event for aerospace and defence manufacturers from around the world.

Boeing, Lockheed Martin and Bell Textron were among the major US companies represented, alongside emerging aerospace technology developers. The event also provides the opportunity for global manufacturers to meet customers, announce aircraft orders and demonstrate new technoloies.

Farnborough’s growing defence presence has become another major attraction, with companies including Anduril Industries showcasing developments in autonomous and military systems during the 2026 event.

Farnborough organisers predict earliest-ever sell out

Gareth Rogers, CEO of Farnborough International, said: “The exceptional demand for Farnborough International Airshow 2028 demonstrates how much businesses value the event as an opportunity to connect with international customers, showcase innovation on a global scale and develop new partnerships for future collaboration.

“With 93% of exhibition and chalet space already sold and reserved just four months after our last edition, we are on track for the earliest sell-out in our show’s history, a clear vote of confidence in Farnborough’s role as a global platform for aerospace, defence and space.”

For more information, visit the Farnborough International Airshow website.

The post Azul opens Amazon crew shuttle with 19-seat Cessna SkyCourier appeared first on AGN.

]]> Azul Conecta’s first Cessna 408 SkyCourier is flying Petrobras workers in Brazil’s Amazonas state. Azul will also sell tickets on two weekly flights linking Manaus, Coari and Carauari.

The 19-seat twin turboprop, registered PS-ENE, entered service on 3 November 2026. Azul Conecta chief executive Vitor Cordeiro told CNN Brasil that the airline expects its second SkyCourier in the first half of 2027. Azul is looking at other routes for the aircraft.

Azul plans public flights via Coari

Azul won a four-year contract to fly Petrobras workers with a flight taxi service following a tender. The flights serve Porto Urucu, Coari and Carauari. The Petrobras contract helped make the SkyCourier purchase possible, Cordeiro told Brazil’s UOL. 

Petrobras has produced oil and gas at Urucu since 1988. Its gas processing plant is in the municipality of Coari. The company uses the Coari River terminal to ship crude oil and liquefied petroleum gas produced at Urucu.

Azul plans to sell seats on two of the aircraft’s weekly flights. On Fridays, it will fly from Carauari to Manaus via Coari. On Mondays, it will fly the reverse route from Manaus to Carauari, with a stop in Coari. Manaus will be the operating base for pilots, mechanics and ground staff.

A step up from the Grand Caravan

The SkyCourier gives Azul Conecta more than twice the capacity of its nine-seat Cessna Grand Caravans. 

“We already have markets that are mature enough to go beyond nine seats,” Cordeiro told UOL. Some of those routes still draw too few passengers for a 72-seat ATR 72.

Azul looked at three aircraft before choosing the SkyCourier, according to UOL, including the Let L-410 Turbolet and De Havilland Canada DHC-6 Twin Otter. 

Cordeiro told UOL that Azul can go longer between some maintenance tasks on the Cessna, which is helpful in Manaus, located far from Brazil’s main maintenance centres. Azul already operates Textron’s Caravans, and its experience with the manufacturer also influenced the decision.

Azul flies the Caravan to Barcelos, where visiting anglers often bring bulky fishing gear. Cordeiro told UOL the SkyCourier has more room for that equipment. The passenger SkyCourier has a 5.27-cubic-metre baggage hold rated for up to 680 kg, according to Textron Aviation’s specifications.

Cordeiro also pointed to the wider cabin, large passenger door and steps as passenger benefits compared to smaller aircraft. Cordeiro told CNN Brasil that Azul was still working out what it costs to fly the SkyCourier. He said it had used less fuel than the airline expected in its early operations.

An aircraft designed for passengers and freight

Brazil’s civil aviation regulator ANAC certified the SkyCourier in 2023.

“The Cessna SkyCourier’s high payload capacity, short takeoff and landing capability, and cost-efficiency make it a great choice for operators in Brazil,” Lannie O’Bannion, senior vice president, Global Sales and Flight Operations, said at the time of the announcement. “The aircraft’s versatility and performance equip customers in the region with smart solutions for their unique missions and circumstances.”

In 2025, Brazilian charter operator Cleiton Táxi Aéreo took delivery of the first SkyCourier in South America. Its aircraft came with a gravel kit for unpaved runways and a conversion kit that lets the operator switch between 19 passenger seats, nine seats with room for cargo, and an all-cargo layout. Brazil’s aviation regulator approved a mixed passenger-and-cargo configuration that year.

]]> Philippine Airlines (PAL) has finalised its order with Boeing for 15 787-10 Dreamliner aircraft, with options to purchase five more as the carrier gains greater visibility on booking demand for its long-haul flights. 

The order is the Filipino flag carrier’s largest ever widebody purchase, and fulfills a commitment announced in July 2026.

Philippine Airlines adds largest member of 787 family 

The 787-10 is the largest member of the 787 family and can seat up to 375 passengers in a two-class configuration. 

It adds to a growing list of widebody types within the PAL fleet. The carrier currently operates the Airbus A350 and A330, and Boeing 777. 

Boeing said the wide-bodies would support the airline’s fleet modernisation and expansion plans, adding capacity and efficiency to its medium- and long-haul network.

The original agreement was announced during the Farnborough International Airshow in July. 

Modernising and expanding PAL’s fleet

Lucio C. Tan III, President and Chief Operating Officer of PAL Holdings, said: “The Boeing 787-10 will play an important role in our plans to modernise and expand our fleet. The post Embraer E195-E2 tested with low-sulphur fuel to tackle contrails appeared first on AGN.

]]> An Embraer E195-E2 has operated a series of research flights over Germany to investigate whether low-sulphur jet fuel, combined with modern engines, can reduce the formation of climate-warming contrails.

The IGNITE-X campaign, led by the German Aerospace Centre (DLR), used a Falcon 20E research aircraft to fly behind the E195-E2 and sample its exhaust plume. 

DLR’s Falcon 20E followed the E195-E2 over test areas in Bavaria and Saxony, collecting samples at different stages of plume development. 

Embraer announced its participation in the tests, which took place in October and November 2026. Researchers are now analysing the data gathered to establish whether changes in fuel composition translate into fewer ice crystals in contrails.

Why sulphur content matters

Contrails form when hot, moist engine exhaust meets cold air, creating ice crystals. Some crystals can linger and spread into clouds that trap heat and contribute to global warming.

As conventional jet fuel cools in the exhaust, its sulphur content forms sulphuric acid particles that can form ice crystals. While soot is still the main source of the crystals which create contrails, researchers are testing whether low-sulphur fuel can reduce contrails, especially in modern engines that produce little soot.

The research used an Embraer E195-E2 equipped with Pratt & Whitney PW1900G geared turbofan engines. The aircraft flew with conventional kerosene and a specially manufactured, certified low-sulphur fuel to allow comparisons under operational flight conditions.

Research aircraft measures emissions in flight

DLR’s Falcon 20E followed the E195-E2, taking exhaust measurements. During close-range measurements, the Falcon flew within 30 metres of the Embraer jet, while other measurements were taken at distances of 10 to 30 kilometres. 

The campaign included about four weeks of ground and flight tests. At Manching military airfield, researchers tested each engine separately at settings ranging from idle to take-off power. A probe measured tiny exhaust particles, allowing researchers to compare emissions from both engines under different conditions.

“We are measuring the emissions directly within the exhaust plume – this is both scientifically and operationally extremely challenging. The test procedure provides unique insights into the potential for reducing emissions. These innovative and, at the same time, challenging tests with our international stakeholders are the result of an exceptionally committed, trusting and inspiring collaboration between applied research and industry,” said Markus Fischer, DLR Divisional Board Member for Aeronautics.

The international project also involved Pratt & Whitney, Aerodyne Research and Missouri University of Science and Technology. Embraer says its participation will help researchers understand the relationship between fuel characteristics, engine performance and contrail formation.

“The E195-E2 was designed to deliver outstanding efficiency and lower emissions, making it an ideal platform for advancing research into the future of sustainable aviation,” said Cleiton Silva, Vice President of Technology Development and Eletronic Equipments at Embraer. “Through our participation in IGNITE-X, we are working alongside leading research institutions and industry partners to better understand the relationship between fuel characteristics, engine performance, and contrail formation. This collaboration reinforces Embraer’s commitment to supporting science-based solutions that contribute to a more sustainable and environmentally responsible aviation sector.”

Early emissions findings are not yet a contrail result

DLR researchers have reported preliminary indications of low soot emissions from the engines and fewer sulphur-containing liquid particles when the low-sulphur fuel was used. However, the team has not yet completed its assessment of how these changes affect ice-crystal numbers or the climate impact of contrails.

Fewer particles in exhaust do not necessarily mean fewer persistent contrails or less warming. The results also depend on temperature, humidity and how the exhaust plume develops.

This research may help identify ways to reduce contrails, supporting other efforts to cut aviation’s carbon dioxide emissions. If it shows a clear benefit, changes to fuel and engine technology could help limit aviation’s climate impact.

DLR says the flight and ground measurements are now being evaluated. 

How IGNITE-X fits into wider contrail research

IGNITE-X is part of a growing effort to understand and reduce aviation’s non-CO₂ climate effects. Earlier research has examined whether changing the fuel itself can reduce the particles around which contrail ice crystals form. In the ECLIF3 programme, Airbus, DLR, Rolls-Royce and Neste tested 100% sustainable aviation fuel on an Airbus A350 and found reductions in both soot particles and contrail ice crystals.

Other studies are looking at where aircraft fly rather than what they burn. In March 2026, AGN reported that American Airlines and Google had tested AI-assisted contrail avoidance across transatlantic operations. Of 2,400 flights assessed, 112 followed suggested avoidance routes and produced 62% less contrail formation than a control group, with no statistically significant difference in fuel burn. 

The potential benefit is significant. A September 2026 study by Klima Consulting for Transport & Environment (T&E) estimated that cutting contrail warming by half could prevent around 0.025°C of global warming by 2050 and 0.049°C by 2070. The same research suggested that a small share of flights accounts for most contrail warming, making targeted interventions potentially more effective than trying to prevent every visible trail.

]]> Canada’s Snowbirds have brought 55 years of flying the CT-114 Tutor to a close, returning to Moose Jaw for a farewell flypast before their familiar red-and-white jets enter retirement.

The team’s final scheduled public appearance came on November 15, when nine Tutors flew over Calgary’s McMahon Stadium ahead of the 113th Grey Cup, Canadian football’s championship game. Their homecoming flypast on November 16 provided one last farewell to the Saskatchewan community that has supported generations of Snowbirds personnel.

“Every pilot, technician and team member who has worn the Snowbirds patch has called Moose Jaw home,” the team shared.

“You’ve welcomed every new team, cheered us on through every season and stood by us in the hardest moments. It has been an honour to represent Moose Jaw to North America, and to carry your name with us everywhere we flew … Thank you, Moose Jaw, for 55 incredible years. “

The retirement ends more than six decades of Canadian military service for the homegrown jet. It also begins a prolonged absence for the Snowbirds, whose eventual return will involve a different aircraft — and a switch from jet power to propellers.

Snowbirds return to Moose Jaw for final Tutor flypast

On November 15, nine Snowbirds Tutors flew over Calgary’s McMahon Stadium ahead of the 113th Grey Cup, as the Edmonton Elks and Montreal Alouettes prepared to contest Canadian football’s championship.

The CFL proudly welcomes the final flight of the iconic Canadian Forces Snowbirds to Canada’s biggest championship celebration – the 113th Grey Cup in Calgary, AB https://t.co/dI40Kt99w3

— CFL (@CFL) September 3, 2026

The flypast marked the team’s final scheduled public appearance with the aircraft, giving the jets a national sporting send-off before their journey home to Moose Jaw.

In a video message shared by the CFL, team leader Major Maciej Hatta thanked the nation for its support of the Snowbirds: “Thank you Canada, for 55 years of support. It’s been an honour serving our great nation.”

Following the final public appearance of the Snowbirds, today the team headed home.

Flying in from Calgary, the team headed straight to Moose Jaw, but took a wide approach from the north, turning due south to fly down the length of Main Street at around 2,500 feet. The Tutors took a wide circuit around the city before heading south to the base.

On approach to the 15 Wing base at Bushell Park, the jets were joined by a pair of PC-21 turboprop trainers, known in Canada as the CT-157 Siskin II, painting a remarkable picture of the past and the future together.

The Snowbirds celebrated the aircraft, saying, “To the CT-114 Tutor: thank you. You’re a Canadian-built jet that has done more than anyone ever asked of you. You carried generations of pilots through thousands of shows, in every kind of weather, from coast to coast to coast. You were reliable, graceful and unmistakably ours. Few aircraft have ever been so loved.”

As the RCAF closes the door on a five and a half decade history with the Tutor, the Snowbirds face an uncertain future, with the team unlikely to return to flying displays before the 2030s.

The Canadian-built jet trainer that became a national symbol

The Tutor began as Canadair’s CL-41, a privately developed jet trainer intended to win an order from the Royal Canadian Air Force. Designed and manufactured in Montreal, it was the company’s first aircraft developed from scratch rather than adapted from an existing design.

Test pilot Ian MacTavish took the prototype into the air on January 13, 1960. Canada ordered 190 production aircraft in September 1961, with deliveries beginning in 1963. In Canadian military service, the aircraft became the CT-114 Tutor.

Its side-by-side cockpit placed instructor and student alongside each other, with matching controls allowing the instructor to demonstrate techniques or intervene. The small, single-engine jet would become a crucial pillar of Canadian pilot training, serving in that role until 2000.

Its public profile grew through aerobatics. Tutors equipped the Golden Centennaires display team during Canada’s centennial celebrations in 1967, before becoming the aircraft of the Snowbirds in 1971. The team has never flown another aircraft type.
